Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 58, verse 1:

﴿God has indeed heard the speech of her who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to God. And God hears your mutual dialogue. Indeed God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.﴾

[p. 7]
The verses on the legal rulings of ẓihār (the pre-Islamic repudiation formula by which a husband compared his wife to his mother's back) open with mention of the occasion of their revelation. This honours the woman who directed her complaint to God, Exalted is He, for she did not fall short in seeking justice for her own rights and the rights of her children. She did not accept the arrogance of her husband, who hastened to what would scatter his family's order without insight or deliberation. It also teaches the women of the Islamic community, and its men, the obligation to defend its interests.

This is the case of the woman Khawlah, or Khuwaylah (diminutive), or Jamilah, daughter of Malik ibn Tha'labah, or daughter of Dulayj (diminutive), of the clan of 'Awf. Some have said she was of the Khazraj, since she was from the sub-clans of 'Awf ibn Malik ibn al-Khazraj, among the Ansar, and was married to Aws ibn al-Samit al-Khazraji, brother of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit.

It is said that the cause of this incident was that her husband saw her while she was praying, and she had a beautiful body. When she finished her prayer he wanted her, but she refused. He became angry, and his character had already become bad, so he said to her: "You are to me like the back of my mother."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "This was in the Jahiliyyah, a permanent prohibition on the woman." That is, the Muslims in Madinah acted upon it with the knowledge of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his approval of the people's practice, until it became an established ruling. Khawlah came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and mentioned this to him. He said to her: "You have become forbidden to him." She said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I have young children. If I give them to him they will be lost, and if I give them to myself they will go hungry." He said: "I have nothing concerning your matter." She said: "O Messenger of God, he did not mention divorce. He is the father of my children and the dearest of people to me." He said: "You have become forbidden to him." She said: "I complain to God of my poverty and my grief." Whenever the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, "You have become forbidden to him," she cried out and complained to God. So God revealed these verses.

This hadith was narrated by Dawud (Abu Dawud) in the Book of Ẓihār in summary form, with a sound chain of transmission (isnad). As for the detailed account of the story, it comes from the narrations of the people of tafsir and of the occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul), some of which add to others. al-Tabari has compiled them thoroughly with their chains going back to Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Abu al-'Aliyah, and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. All of them agree that the woman who pleaded was Khawlah, or Khuwaylah, or Jamilah, and that her husband was Aws ibn al-Samit.

Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi related a hadith on ẓihār in another case, attributed to Salamah ibn Sakhr al-Bayadi, resembling the case of Khawlah: he made ẓihār against his wife during Ramadan, then his desire overcame him and he had intercourse with her, and he asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for a ruling on this, through to the end of the story. However, neither of them mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning it.

Ibn 'Atiyyah attributed to al-Naqqash that the verse was revealed because of the case of Salamah, but this is not known from anyone other than him. I think this is a confusion between the two cases. How could that be correct, when the plain wording of the verse says that the questioner is a woman, while in the hadith of Salamah ibn Sakhr it is he himself who asks?

The particle (qad), originally, is a particle of confirmation of the report, one of the particles of emphasis of a statement. But the address here is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and no doubt lingers in him that God knows what the woman who argued about her husband had said. Thus it is determined that the particle (qad) here is used to express anticipation (tawaqquʿ), that is, to indicate the occurrence of what the listener expects. al-Kashshaf says: "Because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the woman who pleaded were both expecting that God would hear her argument and her complaint and send down what would relieve her."

The meaning of the anticipation that the particle (qad) signals in such a context reduces to treating the one who expects something to happen, out of his intense longing for it, as if he were a doubtful seeker. Thus the affirmation of the report is a departure from the apparent sense for a rhetorical purpose, as they said concerning the emphasis of the statement by (inna) in God's words ﴿And do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they are to be drowned﴾ [Hud: 37]. The one who did not ask is treated as the one who asks, since what hints at the statement is presented to him, so he anticipates it like a seeking, doubtful person. For this reason al-Radi, in his commentary on al-Kafiyah, affirmed definitively that (qad) must always carry the sense of confirmation, and then other meanings are added to it in some places.

The hearing (sama') in His words "heard" means acceptance of what is sought and response to it, as indicated by the anticipatory (qad) preceding it, since what is anticipated is the answering of her complaint.

The woman has been brought forward under the description of the relative clause (she who pleads) to honour her argument and her complaint, because they demonstrate her sincere reliance upon the mercy of her Lord toward her, her children, and her husband.

Mujadalah (pleading) means argument and reasoning. It was discussed earlier in His words ﴿They argue with you concerning the truth after it has become clear﴾ [al-Anfal: 6], in Surah al-Anfal.

[p. 9]
Al-ishtikaʾ (complaint) is an intensified form of al-shakwa, which is mentioning what has harmed one. It is said: shakā, tashakkā, and ishtakā, and the most intensive of them is ishtakā. Most often, complaining is aimed at seeking the removal of the harm one complains of, through a judgement, help, or an indication of a means of escape.

The verb of arguing (tajadul) is connected to the phrase "concerning her husband" by supposing an elided noun, known from context, in such a case: that is, "concerning the matter of her husband and his case," as in His words ﴿He argues with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 74], and His words ﴿And do not address Me concerning those who have wronged﴾ [Hud: 37]. This is from the question that is termed in usul al-fiqh the attribution of permissibility and prohibition to objects (idafat al-tahlil wa al-tahrim ila al-a'yan), as in ﴿Prohibited to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3].

Tahawur (mutual dialogue) is a reciprocal form from hara, meaning "to answer." Thus tahawur is the occurrence of an answer from two sides, which requires a mutual exchange between two persons.

The hearing in His words ﴿And God hears your mutual dialogue﴾ is used in its literal sense, which suits the attributes of God, since nothing diverts it from its literal meaning. That God, Exalted is He, knows what passed in the dialogue is well established, and the informing of it is not meant to convey a ruling. Therefore the statement is understood as intended to express concern for that dialogue and to honour it and its great status, because it involves the Prophet's (ﷺ) anticipation of the revelation he would receive, and the woman's anticipation of mercy. Otherwise, the Muslims know that God knows their dialogue.

The clause ﴿And God hears your mutual dialogue﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in ﴿argues with you﴾. The present tense form is used to bring to mind the simultaneity of God's knowledge with their dialogue, adding to the honouring of that dialogue.

The clause ﴿Indeed God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing﴾ is a concluding appendage (tadhyil) to the clause ﴿And God hears your mutual dialogue﴾, meaning: God knows every voice and everything that is seen. Among that is the dialogue of the one who pleads and its occurrence before the Prophet (ﷺ). The repetition of the divine name (Allah) in a place where a pronoun could have been used, three times, serves to cultivate awe and to stir up the magnification of His favour, Exalted is He, and the motives for thanking Him.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 58, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Those of you who repudiate their wives [by saying], "You are to me like the back of my mother," they are not their mothers. Their mothers are only those who gave birth to them. Indeed, they utter a reprehensible word and a falsehood. And indeed God is Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾

[Page 10]

The sentence ﴿Those of you who repudiate their wives﴾ comes as an explanatory elaboration (*bayan*) of the sentence ﴿God has indeed heard the speech of she who pleads with you concerning her husband﴾ [al-Mujadila: 1], and what follows it completes its rulings. This is because it contains a way out of the harm that befell the woman who pleaded, caused by her husband's *zihar*, and it nullifies that harm. It also has the position of an explanatory resumption (*istinaf bayani*) relative to the sentence ﴿God has indeed heard﴾ [al-Mujadila: 1]. The words ﴿God has indeed heard﴾ [al-Mujadila: 1] raise a question in the mind: "What resulted from God's response to the complaint of the woman who pleaded?" The answer is given, containing her way out of it.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read ﴿yaẓẓahharūna﴾ with a fatha on the *ya'* and a shadda on the *ẓa'* and the *hā'*, both with fatha, without an *alif* after the *ẓa'*. The underlying form is *yatazahharūna*, and the *tā'* was assimilated (*idgham*) into the *ẓā'* because their points of articulation are close. Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf read ﴿yuẓāhirūna﴾ with a fatha on the *ya'*, a shadda on the *ẓa'*, an *alif* after it, and no further change. The underlying form is *yatazāharūna*, and the *tā'* was assimilated as above. 'Asim read ﴿yuẓāhirūna﴾ with a damma on the *ya'*, a light *ẓa'* without shadda, an *alif*, and a kasra on the *hā'*, as the present tense of *ẓāhara*.

The verbal noun of this verb occurs only in the patterns *fi'āl* and *mufā'ala*. One says: *ṣadara minhu ẓihārun wa-muẓāharatun* ("there proceeded from him a *ẓihār* and a *muẓāharah*"). They did not use a verbal noun of the pattern *taẓahhur*. Therefore, in Nafi's reading, the verbal noun of the verb is dispensed with by using the verbal noun of its synonym.

Its meaning is that a man says to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother." This was a saying used in the pre-Islamic period (*jahiliyya*), by which they intended to make the prohibition of marrying her permanent and to sever the marital bond. It is derived from *al-ẓahr* (the back), the opposite of *al-baṭn* (the belly), because the one who says to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother," means by it that he has made her forbidden to himself, just as his mother is forbidden to him. The construction of the comparison is attributed to the wife's back, on the supposition of one of her states, namely the state of the known enjoyment (of intercourse). In this prohibition they followed the path of the implicit metaphor (*isti'ara makniyya*), by likening the wife, when her husband approaches her, to a mount (*rāḥila*), and attributing a back to her is an imaginative element (*takhayyul*) of that metaphor. Then the back of the wife is likened to the back of his mother, that is, in one of his conditions, namely the state of the known enjoyment. The likened element (*al-mushabbah*) is made to be the wife's person, while what is intended is the most specific of her states, which is the state of approaching her. This leads to the attribution of rulings to persons.

So the underlying sense is: "Your approach is like the approach to the back of my mother," that is, her particular mounting. In this formula there is an ellipsis, and the appearance of the letters of the word *ẓahr* within the forms *ẓihār* or *muẓāharah* points to the formula of prohibition, which is "You are to me like the back of my mother," by way of allusion to that formula, in the manner of what is used in *naḥt* (word-blending, the formation of a single word from parts of several words). It is not truly *naḥt*, because *naḥt* involves letters drawn from several words.

The exegetes (*al-mufassirūn*) and the lexicographers said: *al-ẓihār* was a divorce in the pre-Islamic period, requiring permanent prohibition.

I suppose that it was a divorce among the people of Yathrib and its surroundings, because of their extensive mixing with the Jews. I do not suppose that it was known among the Arabs of Mecca, Tihama, Najd and elsewhere, and I have not come upon this in their speech. It is enough that it is not mentioned in the Qur'an except in this Medinan passage and in surah al-Ahzab.

What appears to me is that the people of Yathrib devised this formula for the sake of intensifying the prohibition, for they were, before Islam, intermingled with the Jews and adopted their customs. The Jews used to forbid a man to approach his wife from behind, as was mentioned earlier in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So come to your tilth however you wish﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223] in surah al-Baqarah. Therefore the word *ẓahr* came in this formula, and they combined in this formula an aggravation of the prohibition, namely that she is like his mother, nay, like the back of his mother. So it came out as a hideous and atrocious formula.

From the formula "You are to me like the back of my mother," they took its most explicit and most specific word for its purpose, which is the word *ẓahr*. From it they derived the verb with several patterns: one says *ẓāhara min imra'atihi* and *ẓahhara*, like *ḍā'afa* and *ḍa''afa*, and they add to both the *tā'* of reflexive form (*tā' al-muṭāwa'a*). So they say *taẓāhara minhā* and *tazahhara*. This is not of the kind of *naḥt* such as *basmala* (from *bismillāh*) and *hallala* (from *lā ilāha illā Allāh*), because no single letter is derived from all the words in the sentence.

The address in His words ﴿of you﴾ may be to the Muslims, and then mentioning this description serves as a generalization, explaining the meaning of the relative clause in ﴿those who repudiate﴾, lest it be supposed that the relative clause refers to a specific person.

The *min* in ﴿of you﴾ is explanatory (*bayaniyya*), as is its usual function after indefinite pronouns. Thus it is known that this ruling is a general legislation for every one who repudiates. It is not specific to Khawla nor to women like her who were in poverty and had many children.

As for the *min* in His words ﴿from their wives﴾, it is the *min* of origin (*ibtida'iyya*), connected to ﴿repudiate﴾ because the verb includes the meaning of distance. Since it was a divorce, and divorce distances one spouse from the other, the particle of origin was brought in for it, as one says: "He went out from the city."

It has become clear that the common usage in the formula of *ẓihār* is that it includes what indicates the wife, the back and the mother, without attention to the linking elements among these three words, such as verbs and particles, as in: "You are to me like the back of my mother," or "You are to me like the back of my mother," or "Be for me like the back of my mother," or the like.

But if some of the three words are absent, or all of them, such as: "Your face is upon me like the back of my mother," or "like the side of my mother," or "like the back of my grandmother," or "of my daughter," or any speech that conveys the likening of the wife, or the joining of her to one of his female unmarriageable kin, with the intention of prohibiting her approach, then all of that is *ẓihār* according to the most well-known opinions of Malik, his companions, and the majority of jurists. It does not shift to the formula of divorce or prohibition, because God intended to give latitude to people and to avoid holding them to account.

The Qur'an mentioned neither the name of the back nor the name of the mother except out of regard for the formula that was current among people at that time, such that the ruling does not pass from *ẓihār* to the formula of divorce unless it is stripped of those three words in a clear way.

The forms are numerous, and encompassing them is not beneficial. That belongs to the domain of legal opinion (*fatwa*) and is not the path of tafsir.

The sentence ﴿they are not their mothers﴾ is the predicate of ﴿those who﴾. That is: their wives are not their mothers by the saying of one of them, "You are to me like the back of my mother." That is, the husband does not thereby become a mother to the speaker of that statement.

This is a preliminary to annulling the effect of the formula of *ẓihār* on the prohibition of the wife, by indicating that motherhood is real and established, not manufactured by speech, since speech does not change the realities of things. As the Exalted said in surah al-Ahzab: ﴿That is your saying with your mouths﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4]. Therefore it follows here with His words ﴿Their mothers are only those who gave birth to them﴾. That is: the wives who are subject to *ẓihār* do not become mothers by that *ẓihār*, because the reality of motherhood is absent in them, since they did not give birth to those who say, "You are to me like the back of my mother." So they are not forbidden to them. Therefore the restriction (*qaṣr*) in the verse is real (*qaṣr ḥaqiqi*), that is: the prohibition by *ẓihār* is a void matter that is not implied by any cause that would produce it.

[Page 11]

The sentence ﴿Their mothers are only﴾ and so on is positioned as a justification for the sentence ﴿they are not their mothers﴾. It is a justification for the purpose of this statement, I mean the nullification of the prohibition by the word *ẓihār*, since the fact that they are not their mothers is self-evident and does not need justification.

Their practice is reproached further by His words ﴿Indeed, they utter a reprehensible word and a falsehood﴾, as a rebuke for their conduct. That is: although it does not necessitate the prohibition of the woman, it is a reprehensible saying (*munkar*), that is, ugly, because it exposes the sanctity of the mother to hideous imaginings that come to the mind of the hearer when he hears the speech of the one who repudiates: "You are to me like the back of my mother." This is a state required by the mention of the back in His words, "like the back of my mother."

I suppose that the thought which dictated the formula of *ẓihār* to the first one who uttered it was full of anger, which inspires foul speech, like their saying in abuse: "Suck the clitoris of your mother," and this too is a falsehood (*zūr*), because it is a lie, since God did not prohibit her. The Exalted said in surah al-Ahzab: ﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you repudiate [by saying "back of my mother"] your mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4].

The emphasis of the predicate by *inna* and the *lām* serves to draw attention to its heinousness, since people had become accustomed to it, so they were treated as one who doubts whether it is reprehensible or false. In this there is an indication that *ẓihār* was not legislated in any earlier law nor in the law of Islam, and that it was something that the people of the pre-Islamic period devised, as is pointed out by its being counted together with the pre-Islamic falsehoods in the Exalted's words: ﴿God has not made for any man two hearts within his body, nor has He made your wives whom you repudiate your mothers, nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4]. This was mentioned earlier in surah al-Ahzab.

After this rebuke, He joined to it the sentence ﴿And indeed God is Pardoning﴾, as a metaphor (*kināya*) for not holding them accountable for what proceeded from them of *ẓihār* before this verse, since their excuse was that this was a saying they followed their forebears in, and it passed over their tongues without reflection on its implications. As for after the revelation of this verse, the position of the Malikis is that the ruling for pronouncing it is prohibition, as Ibn Rashid al-Qafsi explicitly stated in *al-Lubab*, on the basis of His saying after it: ﴿And these are the limits of God﴾ [al-Mujadila: 4], that the pronouncing of *ẓihār* is a disobedience. Because it is a disobedience, Ibn 'Atiyya interpreted the Exalted's words ﴿And indeed they utter a reprehensible word and a falsehood﴾ accordingly. In the same way al-Qurtubi interpreted the Exalted's words ﴿And these are the limits of God﴾ [al-Mujadila: 4]. Ibn al-Faras said: it is forbidden, and it is not lawful to pronounce it. Its prohibition is indicated by three things. The first: God's denial of the one who does this. The second: that He called it *munkar* and *zūr*, and *zūr* is falsehood, which is forbidden by *ijma'* (scholarly consensus).

[Page 14]

The third: His informing about it that He pardons it and forgives it, and pardon and forgiveness are only for sinners.

The opinions of the Hanafi jurists indicate that *ẓihār* is a disobedience, but none of the Malikis nor the Hanafis described it as a major sin (*kabira*). There is no proof in describing it in the verse as *zūr*, because a lie is not a major sin unless it leads to harm.

Al-Subki in *Jam' al-Jawami'* counted *ẓihār* among the major sins, and al-Mahalli accepted this. The writers said that God named it *zūr*, and *zūr* is a major sin, so the statement that *ẓihār* is a major sin is the opinion of the Shafi'is. But there is room for scrutiny in this, for they did not count lying in absolute terms as a major sin; they only counted false testimony (*shahādat al-zūr*) as a major sin.

The phrase ﴿Pardoning﴾ is followed by ﴿Forgiving﴾. So His words ﴿And indeed God is Pardoning, Forgiving﴾ mean: God has pardoned them and forgiven them, for He is Pardoning and Forgiving, who forgives this and what is greater than it.

*Al-'Afuww* is the one who pardons much. *Al-'afw* is the non-imposition of accountability for an act. That is, a pardon regarding their saying, which is reprehensible and false. *Al-Ghafūr* is the one who forgives much, and *ghufrān* is overlooking one who performs an act for which he deserves to be punished. So mentioning the attribute *Ghafūr* after the attribute *'Afuww* completes the glorification of God, since there is no sin in *ẓihār* where no prohibition had preceded it, and together with the antithesis between two things, *munkar* and *zūr*, and two things, *'afuww* and *ghafūr*.

The emphasis of the predicate in His words ﴿And indeed God is Pardoning, Forgiving﴾ corresponds to the emphasis of its opposite in His words ﴿And indeed they utter a reprehensible word and a falsehood﴾.

And His words ﴿And indeed God is Pardoning, Forgiving﴾ indicate that *ẓihār* after the revelation of this verse is forbidden, and we will mention that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 58, verse 2 (part 2 of 2):

His words, ﴿And indeed Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾, point to the fact that Allah's purpose in this ruling is to ease matters for people. Thus we know that the objective of the Islamic Shari'ah is for the rulings of *zihar* (the pre-Islamic practice of a husband declaring his wife forbidden to him by likening her to his mother's back) to revolve around the axis of lightening and facilitation. On this basis, jurists must proceed in what they issue as legal opinions. Therefore, the principle of *al-akhdh bil-ahwat* (taking the most cautious position) and the principle of *sadd al-dhari'a* (blocking the means that lead to prohibited acts) should not be applied to this matter. Rather, we must follow what the words of Allah, ﴿And indeed they say an evil word and a lie, but indeed Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾, have illuminated for us.

Malik said in *al-Mudawwana* (a major early book of Maliki law): The one who makes *zihar* should not kiss, should not engage in physical intimacy, and should not look at a woman's chest or hair. Al-Baji said in *al-Muntaqa*: Among our companions, some interpreted this as prohibition (*tahrim*), and among them others interpreted it as disliked (*karahiyya*), lest it lead him to sexual intercourse. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i and 'Abd al-Malik.

I say: This is the correct view, because the Qur'an mentioned *al-masis* (touching), which is a *haqiqa shar'iyya* (a technical legal usage) for sexual intercourse. Malik also said: If a man makes *zihar* against four wives with a single formula in a single session, he is only obligated to pay one expiation (*kaffara*), according to Malik's single opinion. According to Abu Hanifa and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i, [he is obligated to pay expiation for each wife].

The purpose of this verse is to nullify the prohibition of the wife against whom the husband makes *zihar*, and to ridicule the people of the Jahiliyya who made *zihar* a prohibition upon the husband regarding the wife against whom he made it.

Allah made the expiation a ransom for this act and a deterrent, so that people would refrain from this statement.

From this same meaning is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever says to his companion, 'Come, let me gamble with you,' let him give charity." That is, whoever has this said by his tongue after Allah has prohibited gambling (*maysir*).

[Page 15]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 58, verse 3:

﴿Those who divorce by zihar from their wives and then retract what they said - the freeing of a slave before they touch one another. That is what you are admonished with, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

It is conjoined to the sentence ﴿Those of you who divorce by zihar from their wives - they are not their mothers﴾ [al-Mujadila: 2]. The subject is repeated in it for the sake of emphasizing the ruling and explicitly naming its people. The expected form of the discourse would have been: "But if they retract what they said, then the freeing of a slave," so that it would be a conjunction with the predicative sentence in His words ﴿they are not their mothers﴾ [al-Mujadila: 2].

The "thumma" (then) conjoins the sentence "they retract" to the sentence "they divorce by zihar." It indicates a gradation in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), an allusion to rebuke for them, in that they returned to what they used to do in the Jahiliyyah after that had been cut off by Islam. For this reason, the verb "they retract" is linked to what indicates their saying the word zihar.

Al-'awd (retraction) is returning to something one left and abandoned, and its origin is returning to the place one departed from; here it is a figurative retraction.

The meaning of ﴿they retract what they said﴾ may be that they retract what they uttered of zihar. This requires that the one who makes zihar is not a zahir (one who makes zihar) unless the word of zihar has proceeded from him a second time after a first. This is how al-Farra' interpreted it. It is related from 'Ali ibn Talha from Ibn 'Abbas that what proceeds from him the first time is pardoned. However, the sound hadith in the case of al-Mujadila repels this apparent meaning, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Aws ibn al-Samit: "Free a slave," as will come in the hadith of Abu Dawud. Thus it is established that expiation is obligatory upon the one who makes zihar from the first time he utters the word of zihar.

It may also be intended that they wish to return to their wives, i.e., they do not love separation and desire to return to marital relations. This interpretation is agreed upon by the jurists, except Dawud al-Zahiri, Bukayr ibn al-Ashajj, and Abu al-'Aliyah. In the Muwatta', Malik said regarding the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿Those who divorce by zihar from their wives and then retract what they said﴾, he said: "I heard that the explanation of this is that a man makes zihar from his wife, then after his zihar he resolves to have intercourse with her and keep her. If he resolves upon that, expiation becomes obligatory upon him; and if he divorces her and does not resolve after his zihar from her to keep her, there is no expiation upon him."

The statements of Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i, and al-Layth revolve around this meaning, with differences in expression that we will not dwell on.

Accordingly, the verb "they retract" has been used to mean intending to return, just as a verb is used to mean intending to return and resolving upon it, not returning in actuality. For if it were returning in actuality, there would be no meaning to the condition that expiation precede touching. Thus the meaning is established: "then they intend to return to what they forbade for themselves; upon them is expiation before they return to it," in the manner of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 6], i.e., when you intend to stand, and His saying ﴿When you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾ [al-Nahl: 98], and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "If you ask, ask Allah, and if you seek help, seek help from Allah."

This is the matter of the occasion of revelation, because the woman only came disputing because she knew that her husband who made zihar from her did not intend to separate from her, as the hadith related on this in the Sunan of Abu Dawud indicates: "From Khuwaylah bint Malik ibn Tha'labah, she said: My husband Aws ibn al-Samit made zihar from me, so I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) complaining to him, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was disputing with me and saying: 'Fear Allah, for he is your cousin.' I did not leave until the Qur'an was revealed. He said: 'Let him free a slave.' She said: 'He does not find one.' He said: 'Then let him fast two consecutive months.' She said: 'He is an old man who has no fasting in him.' He said: 'Then let him feed sixty poor persons.' She said: 'He has nothing to give in charity.' Then at that moment a basket of dates was brought. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I will help him with another basket.' He said: 'You have done well. Go and feed sixty poor persons with them on his behalf, and return to your cousin.'" Abu Dawud said regarding this: she expiated on his behalf without consulting him.

The meaning of "what they said" is what they said with the word zihar, which is what they forbade for themselves of enjoyment, derived from the expression "you are upon me like the back of my mother," because "you are upon me" carries the meaning of "your intimacy and the like is upon me as the back of my mother." From this is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We inherit what he says﴾ [Maryam: 80], i.e., wealth and children, in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And he said: I will surely be given wealth and children﴾ [Maryam: 77]; and His saying ﴿Say: There have certainly come to you messengers before me with clear proofs and with what you have said﴾ [Al 'Imran: 183], i.e., your saying "until he brings us an offering which the fire devours." So the verb "say" in this and similar usages governs a single noun, since it occurs within a quoted sentence; and the choice of expression is for the meaning for which the prohibition occurred. Thus the expression of zihar with the relative pronoun and its relative clause is a concision and a purification of the discourse from explicitly stating it. The meaning is: then they wish to return to enjoying their wives after they had forbidden it for themselves.

It is understood from His saying ﴿then they retract what they said﴾ that whoever does not intend to return to his wife has one of two states: either he intends to divorce her, and he may pronounce another divorce upon her, since Allah nullified that zihar be a divorce; or he intends neither divorce nor return. This one has become prevented from marital intercourse with his wife, harming her, so he has the ruling of ila' (oath of abstention) in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿For those who swear abstention from their wives is a waiting period of four months﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226], and so on. They used to make zihar equivalent to ila', as in the case of Salamah ibn Sakhr al-Bayadi, then al-Zuraqi, in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, who said: "I was a man who had intercourse with women more than others do. When the month of Ramadan came, I feared that I would fall into something harmful to me with my wife..." — with a letter of the second-person prefix [ta'] ... and the apparent reading is that it is vocalized with a kasra — and the tata'ub is falling into evil; so the ba' in his saying (bi) is extra for emphasis — "until morning came, and I made zihar from her until the month of Ramadan ended," the hadith.

The lam in His saying ﴿li-ma qalu﴾ has the meaning of (ila) "to," as in His saying ﴿Because your Lord has inspired her﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 5], and its parallel is His saying ﴿And if they were returned, they would certainly return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28]. I think the original meaning of the lam is causation (al-ta'lil), namely that in such positions, if the verb to which it is attached does not contain the meaning of arrival, the lam is taken in the sense of causation, which is the original, as in ﴿Because your Lord has inspired her﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 5]. What occurs with (ila) in such cases is a figurative usage, treating the one who does the act for its sake as if he were the one arriving at it. If the verb to which the lam is attached does contain the meaning of arrival, like the verb "to return," then its attachment with lam indicates the intention of a meaning in that verb by an implied limitation or an implied complement that suits the particle of causation, as in His saying ﴿Each runs for a specified term﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2], i.e., its continuous running is for its aim of reaching a term it attains. From this is His saying ﴿And if they were returned, they would certainly return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28], i.e., they would repeat its doing; and from it is what is in this verse.

In the Kashshaf, regarding His saying ﴿Each runs for a specified term﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2] in the Surah al-Zumar, it says that it is not like His saying ﴿Each runs to a specified term﴾ [Luqman: 29] in the Surah Luqman; i.e., it is not from the interchange of the two particles, and only one of narrow outlook follows this method; but the two meanings, I mean elevation and specification, both suit the soundness of the purpose, because His saying "ila ajal" means it reaches it, and His saying "li-ajal" means for the attainment of a term, making the running specific to attainment. End of quotation.

So the estimate on this view is: "then they intend to return on account of what they said," i.e., on account of their desire for their wives. The object of the verb "they return" is thus implied by the context: "they return to what they had relinquished of the marital bond," and the verb comes to mean "they regret the separation."

What results from this is that the expiation of zihar was prescribed when the one who makes zihar intends to continue in marital intercourse with his wife, as a remedy for the prohibition he intended, and as a discipline for him upon this corrupt intention and this abominable saying.

On this basis, the understanding of His saying ﴿before they touch one another﴾ is that it means before he touches his wife with touching of enjoyment, before he expiates. It is a kinaya (metonymy) for intercourse in the technical usage of the Qur'an, as He said ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. For this reason the expiation was made the freeing of a neck, because by that neck he ransoms his wife's neck.

Allah has made it an admonition by His saying ﴿That is what you are admonished with﴾. The demonstrative in His saying "dhalikum" refers to the freeing of a neck. Exhortation (al-wa'z) is reminding of good and warning against evil by encouragement or intimidation; that is, the imposition of expiation is an alert for you, so that you avoid touching the woman who was divorced, or continue in separating from her while desiring to return to marital intercourse with her, lest you return to zihar. Allah did not name it expiation here, but the Prophet (ﷺ) named it expiation, as in the hadith of Salamah ibn Sakhr al-Bayadi in the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi. Expiation is indeed a kind of punishment according to one of two views from Malik, and it is the view of al-Shafi'i, related from him by Ibn al-'Arabi in al-Ahkam.

So the one who makes zihar is prohibited from enjoying his wife who was made zihar, i.e., he is prohibited from the bonds of marriage, and that requires the suspension of the marital bond until he expiates, because he obligated himself to that. If he enjoyed her before the full expiation, then let him repent to Allah and seek forgiveness, and the expiation becomes binding on him. The expiation is not multiplied due to enjoyment before the reminder, because it is one cause, so the repetition of its causer does no harm. The expiation was made a deterrent, and for this reason the zihar-maker's intercourse with his wife before expiation is not zina. Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi related the hadith of Salamah ibn Sakhr al-Bayadi that he made zihar from his wife, then had intercourse with her before he expiated, and the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded him with one expiation; this is the view of the majority of scholars. From Mujahid and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi: he owes two expiations.

The detailed rulings of zihar, its formula and other matters, are detailed in the books of jurisprudence.

His saying ﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ is a tadhyil (concluding appendage) to the sentence ﴿That is what you are admonished with﴾, i.e., Allah is Knowing of all that you do of this expiation and other than it.

Concession for one who cannot find a slave to free: he may move on to fasting two consecutive months, because when he cannot find a slave to free, he substitutes for freeing a slave the release of the bond of the wife, and so he is transferred to an expiation in which there is the hardship of the self through patience over the pleasure of food and drink, so as to offset by it the hardship of patience over keeping away from his spouse, which he had imposed upon himself by zihar. Fasting thus became a second degree, close to the degree of freeing a slave in its suitability.

The condition ﴿before they touch one another﴾ [al-Mujadila: 3] is repeated to indicate that touching is permitted only after the completion of the fast, so that one should not suppose that merely beginning the fast suffices for returning to sexual enjoyment.

﴿But whoever is not able﴾, i.e., because of his incapacity or weakness, God has granted him the concession to move on to feeding sixty needy people in place of fasting. Feeding is a third degree, which removes from sixty needy people the pain of hunger in exchange for what he had imposed upon himself of the hardship of keeping away from his pleasures. It was specified as sixty needy people by analogy with the expiation for deliberately breaking a day's fast in Ramadan, on the common ground that both are expiations for a fast, so the expiation was proportionate to what it expiates, arranged in a fitting order. The quantity of food has been left general in the verse, being content with calling it "feeding" (iṭ‘ām), so it is understood according to what people intend by food, which is one satisfying meal, as is customary in the usage of the verb ṭa‘ima. Our scholars therefore understood it as that which satisfies the hungry, so it is measured for each people according to what satisfies the customary hungry.

On this, Mālik, may God have mercy on him, has two reports: one is that it is one mudd for each needy person by the mudd of the Prophet ﷺ; the second is that it is two mudds, or nearly two mudds, which is a mudd by the mudd of Hisham ibn Isma'il al-Makhzumi, governor of Madina, and its measure is two mudds minus a third of a mudd. Ashhab said: I said to Mālik: Does the measure of satisfaction differ between us and you? He said: Yes, the satisfying measure for us is one mudd by the mudd of the Prophet ﷺ, and the satisfying measure for you is more; that is, because the Prophet ﷺ invoked blessing upon the people of Madina. His statement implies that feeding in Madina should be one mudd by the mudd of the Prophet ﷺ, like the expiation for breaking the fast in Ramadan. So how did Mālik make it two mudds or two-thirds of a mudd? He said: If one feeds a mudd and a half of a mudd, it suffices. It is therefore established that doubling the quantity in feeding carries the sense of punishment for what he did; otherwise there is no evidence for it from text or analogy. Abu al-Hasan al-Qabisi said: The people of Madina adopted the mudd of Hisham for the expiation of zihar only as a severity against those who engage in zihar, of whom God testified that they utter an objectionable word and falsehood. This is among what was established by the practice of the people of Madina.

Abu Hanifa measured the satisfying amount as two mudds by the mudd of the Prophet ﷺ, perhaps because he considered satisfaction in most regions other than Madina. Al-Shafi‘i measured it as one mudd for each needy person, by analogy with what is established in the Sunna regarding the expiation for breaking the fast and the expiation for oaths.

The condition ﴿before they touch one another﴾ [al-Mujadila: 3] was not mentioned with feeding, being content with its mention alongside freeing a slave and fasting two months; and because feeding is a substitute for fasting and divisible into a number equal to the days of fasting. This is the view of the majority of jurists.

It is reported from Abu Hanifa that it is not a condition for feeding that it occur before they touch one another.

Further, if intercourse occurs before the expiation or before its completion, nothing else follows from it except that he is sinful, since no other consequence can follow from it. This is what the hadith of Salama ibn Sakhr explains, who complained to the Prophet ﷺ that he had had intercourse with his wife after having made zihar against her, so he commanded him not to return to the like of that until he had made expiation. This is the view of the majority of jurists, while Mujahid said that he owes two expiations.

The explicit wording of the verse is that the consecutiveness of the fasting is a condition for the expiation; accordingly, if he breaks the fast in its course without excuse, he must repeat it.

He must not touch his wife until he completes the two consecutive months. If he touches her during the two months, he is sinful and must repeat the two months. Al-Shafi‘i said: If the intercourse takes place at night, the consecutiveness is not invalidated, because the night is not a place for fasting; this is what runs according to analogy and according to the implication of the hadith of Salama ibn Sakhr.

As for his being sinful by touching before completing the expiation, that is a separate question. It is strange that Abu Bakr ibn al-‘Arabi said of al-Shafi‘i's statement that it is the speech of one who has not tasted the flavour of jurisprudence, because intercourse occurring during the fast is not the place permitted for the expiation, for it is intercourse of transgression; so there must be compliance with the command to a fast in which there is no intercourse during its course. End quote.

Al-Miskin: one who is in extreme poverty; this was discussed earlier in Surat Bara'a.

If the one who makes zihar is able to perform some of the kinds of expiation but refuses to make expiation, his zihar turns into an oath of abstinence (īlā'). If the woman is not content to remain in that state, he has the term of the īlā'; if the term expires, his wife is divorced against him if she requests divorce. If he is incapable of all the kinds of expiation, he is like one incapable of intercourse after it has occurred from him; the marriage bond remains between the one who made zihar and his wife, and he may not approach her until he makes expiation.

The Prophet ﷺ commanded that the expiation of Salama ibn Sakhr be paid from the public treasury (bayt al-mal). Therefore it is incumbent upon the rulers to pay on behalf of the incapable the expiation for his zihar. If that is impossible, the apparent view is that the expiation falls from him, that he returns to intercourse with his wife, and the expiation remains a debt upon him in his obligation, because God nullified the divorce of zihar.

﴿That is that you may believe in God and His Messenger; and these are the limits of God. And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment.﴾

The reference is to the rulings mentioned: that is, what has been mentioned is so that you may believe in God and His Messenger, i.e., that you may believe with complete faith by complying with what God and His Messenger have commanded you, so do not mix the deeds of faith with the deeds of the people of ignorance. This is an increase in the condemnation of zihar, and a warning to the Muslims against committing it in the future. Or that transfer is from the hardship of separation caused by the utterance of zihar to the concession of not counting it and of release from it through expiation, to facilitate faith for you. This is in the sense of His saying ﴿and He has not placed upon you any hardship in religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78].

"That you may believe" is the predicate of the demonstrative noun, and the lam is for causation. Since what is referred to is fasting two months or feeding sixty needy people in place of freeing a slave, what is given as the cause for freeing a slave extends to fasting and feeding, and what is given as the cause for fasting and feeding extends to freeing a slave. Thus it conveys that each of freeing a slave, fasting two months, and feeding sixty needy people includes both causes, which are admonition and faith in God and His Messenger.

The demonstrative in ﴿and these are the limits of God﴾ refers to what was referred to by "that", and the feminine demonstrative is used for it in view of the predication with the word "limits" (ḥudūd), which is a plural that permits the feminine of its demonstrative, just as it permits the feminine of its pronoun. Similar is His saying ﴿These are the limits of God, so do not transgress them﴾ [al-Baqara: 229] in Surat al-Baqara.

The clause ﴿And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾ completes the clause ﴿That is that you may believe in God and His Messenger﴾; that is, that ruling, namely the nullification of the prohibition by zihar, is the ruling of Islam. As for what they were upon, it is from the remnants of the Jahiliyya; it is the custom of a people for whom there is a painful punishment for disbelief and what has arisen from it of falsehoods. So zihar is a law of the Jahiliyya. This is like His saying ﴿Indeed, the postponing [of a sacred month] is an increase in disbelief﴾ [al-Tawba: 37], because the polytheists instituted it and it was not part of the Hanifiyya.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 58, verse 5:

﴿Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger will be humiliated, just as those before them were humiliated.﴾ When the mention of the disbelievers came up, and the mention of Allah's limits (ḥudūd) came up, and there were hypocrites among the polytheists in Medina, the discourse shifted to threatening them and alerting the Muslims to be on guard against them.

Al-muḥādda (opposition) means hostility and enmity. This verb was chosen here because the discourse follows the mention of Allah's limits, for muḥādda is derived from ḥadd (limit), since each of two opponents is as if in a limit contrary to the other's limit, similar to what was said: that enmity (ʿadāwa) is derived from ʿudwat al-wādī (the bank of the valley), because each of the two enemies resembles one who is on a different bank from the other.

It was also said: al-mushāqqa (opposition) is derived from al-shiqqa (side), because each of two opposed parties is as if on a side different from the other's side.

By them is meant those who oppose the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who was sent with the religion of Allah, so opposing him is opposing Allah.

Al-kabt means disgrace and humiliation. The verb kubitū is used here in the sense of a threat, meaning "they will be humiliated." It is expressed in the past tense to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence, since it proceeds from One whose report is not disputed, like ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Naḥl: 1], and because it is confirmed by comparison with what happened to their likes. The indication of this is the emphasis of the statement with "inna," for if the speech were a report of a humiliation that had already occurred, there would be no reason to emphasize the report, since no one disputes what has occurred. This is further clarified by His words ﴿as those before them were humiliated﴾, meaning those who opposed Allah in the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq). Its mention has preceded in Surah al-Aḥzāb. As for the hypocrites in it, the relative clause "from before them" refers to those before them from among the people of hypocrisy, whom they knew.
