﴿And for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment﴾
It is conjoined to the clause ﴿they will be humiliated, just as those before them were humiliated﴾, meaning: for them, after the humiliation, there is a humiliating punishment in the Hereafter.

The definite article in al-kāfirīn is the definition of the genus, so as to encompass all disbelievers.

He described their punishment as "humiliating" to match their threat of being humiliated (kabt), which is disgrace and abasement.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 58, verse 6:

﴿On the Day when Allah will resurrect them all together and inform them of what they did. Allah has enumerated it, though they have forgotten it. And Allah is Witness over all things.﴾

It is permissible that "yawma" (on the day) is an adverbial complement (zarf) related to the implied verb (al-kawn al-muqaddar) in the predicate of the subject in ﴿And for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment﴾ [al-Mujadila: 5].

It is also permissible that it is related to "muhin" (humiliating), and it is permissible that it is in the accusative as an object (maf'ul bihi) of a verb whose estimated form is: "Mention" (udhkur), as an honouring of that day and a terrifying of them. This is common in the names of time that occur in the Qur'an. It has already been discussed in His Exalted saying ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successive authority"﴾ [al-Baqara: 30] in Surat al-Baqara.

The plural pronoun refers back to ﴿those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Mujadila: 5] and ﴿those before them﴾ [al-Mujadila: 5]. For this reason the word expressing totality, "jami'an" (all together), is used as a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun.

His saying ﴿and He will inform them of what they did﴾ is a threat of exposing their hypocrisy on the Day of Resurrection. In it is a metonymy (kinaya) for the recompense for their deeds.

The sentence ﴿Allah has enumerated it, though they have forgotten it﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial state (hal) relating to "ma 'amilu" (what they did).

The purpose of the state is what is conjoined to it by His saying "though they have forgotten it," because that is the locus of the lesson. Thereby the state is establishing (mu'assisa), not merely emphasizing (mu'akkida) its governing element, which is "yunabbi'uhum." That is, Allah knew it in detailed knowledge from now on, while they had forgotten it. This is a recording against them that they are negligent of the great matter, and that is from delusion, i.e., they forgot it in this world, let alone the Hereafter. So when they are informed of it, they marvel. He, Exalted, said: ﴿And the Book will be placed, and you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it, and they will say, "Oh woe to us! What is this Book that leaves nothing small or great except that it has enumerated it?" And they will find what they did present﴾ [al-Kahf: 49].

The sentence ﴿And Allah is Witness over all things﴾ is a concluding summation (tadhyil). And "al-Shahid" means the one who knows observable matters.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 58, verse 7:

﴿Have you not considered that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth? There is no private conversation of three but that He is their fourth, nor of five but that He is their sixth, nor of less than that or more but that He is with them wherever they are. Then He will inform them of what they did on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾.

This is an initial resumptive statement (isti'naf ibtida'i), a transition (takhallus) from His saying ﴿Allah has enumerated it, though they have forgotten it﴾ [al-Mujadila: 6] to the mention of Allah's knowledge of the conditions of the hypocrites and their allies among the Jews. The hypocrites would hold secret consultations (yunaji) among themselves in order to show the Muslims the mutual affection of some hypocrites for others. By their private conferring they gave the impression that they were a group with a single purpose and a single word. Although they outwardly professed Islam, they wished to have awe in the hearts of the Muslims, by which they would protect themselves from harm if some of them were accused of hypocrisy, or if one of them let slip something that revealed his hypocrisy; the believers would then not dare to harm him, knowing that he had an inner circle (bitana) who would defend him. Whenever Muslims passed by them, they would look at them, so the passers-by would suppose that some event or calamity had occurred. The Muslims at that time were constantly anticipating war with the polytheists, so they would imagine that the conversation of those who conferred privately concerned the nearness of the enemy or a defeat of the Muslims in the expeditions (sara-ya) in which they went out. Thus these verses were revealed to make the hypocrites aware of Allah's knowledge of what they confer about, and that He informs His Messenger ﷺ of their inner intentions, so that they would desist from plotting against the Muslims.

This verse is a preparation for His saying ﴿Have you not considered those who were forbidden from private conferring?﴾ [al-Mujadila: 8], and so on.

"Alam tara" here is from the cognitive sense of seeing (al-ru'ya al-'ilmiyya), because Allah's knowledge is not seen, and the verbal noun (al-masdar) takes the place of the object. The estimate is: Have you not considered Allah as knowing?

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ encompasses what is seen and what is heard, so it is more general than His saying ﴿and Allah is Witness over all things﴾ [al-Mujadila: 6], because that is specific to the knowledge of what is observed, whereas the purpose with which this sentence opens is the knowledge of what is heard.

The clause ﴿there is no private conversation ... ﴾ to the end is a partial substitute (badal al-ba'd min al-kull), since the meaning of His saying ﴿but that He is their fourth﴾, ﴿but that He is their sixth﴾, and ﴿but that He is with them﴾ is that He is informed of what they confer about, so it is as though He, exalted is He, were a confidant with them.

"Ma" is negating. "Yakunu" is the imperfect of the complete (tamma) kana, "min" is an additional particle in the negation for the purpose of generality, and "najwa" is in the sense of the subject of "yakunu".

The majority of readers read "yakunu" with the masculine third-person prefix (ya'), because the feminine marking of "najwa" is not real, so its verb may be treated according to the original masculine form, especially since it is separated from its subject by the additional particle "min". Abu Ja'far read it with the feminine ta', observing the feminine form of its wording.

"Najwa" is the verbal noun of "najahu", meaning when he confided to him in secret. "Thalathatin" is the genitive complement of "najwa". That is: there is no private conferring of three people among men except that Allah is informed of them as their fourth, nor of five except as their sixth, nor less or more except that He is as one of them. The pronouns of the third person refer to "thalatha" and to "khamsa" and to "dhalika" and "akthar".

The purpose of this report is warning and threat.

The specification of the numbers three and five is mentioned because some of those in private conference, on whose account the verse was revealed, were allied groups, some of three and some of five. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is not fixed and the number is not intended.

In al-Kashshaf, from Ibn 'Abbas: it was revealed concerning Rabi'a and Habib, the two sons of 'Amr ibn 'Umayr from Thaqif, and Safwan ibn Umayya al-Sulami, ally of Banu Asad, who were conversing. One of them said: Do you think Allah knows what we say? The other said: He knows some of it and does not know some of it. The third said: If He knows some of it, then He knows all of it. End of quotation. I have not seen this in other than al-Kashshaf, and there is no connection between this and the threat in His saying ﴿then He will inform them of what they did on the Day of Resurrection﴾, for those three were Muslims and were counted among the Companions. It seems that this is a confusion by the narrator between the occasion of revelation of the verse ﴿And you did not used to conceal [yourselves] lest your hearing or your sight or your skins testify against you﴾ [Fussilat: 22] in the surah of Fussilat, as in Sahih al-Bukhari, and this verse. The names of three others who were in Medina were combined, because the verse is Medinan; the verse of private conferring refers to the conferring of the hypocrites, or to them and the Jews, according to Ibn 'Abbas.

The exception in ﴿but that He is their fourth﴾, ﴿but that He is their sixth﴾, ﴿but that He is with them﴾ is a branching (mufarra') from states and conditions indicated by His saying "yakunu". The clauses that follow the exceptive particle are in positions of circumstantial clauses (ahwal). The estimate is: there is no occurrence in the private conferring of three in a state of other than His knowledge of them and His being informed of them, except the state in which Allah is informed of them.

The repetition of the negative particle in the conjoined elements after the negated item is an Arabic stylistic feature, especially where each of the conjoined items has an exception.

The majority read "wa-la akthara" with the accusative on "akthar", coordinated on the wording of "najwa". Ya'qub read it with the nominative, coordinated on the position (mahall) of "najwa", since it is genitive by an additional prepositional particle. "Ayna ma" is compounded from "ayna", which is a locative adverb, and the additional "ma". "Ayna" is annexed to the clause "kanu", that is, in whatever place they were in it. Its parallel is His saying ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid: 4] in the surah of al-Hadid.

"Thumma" indicates a graded delay, because their being informed of what they said and what they did in the world on the Day of Resurrection is a stronger proof of the vastness of Allah's knowledge than His knowledge of their talk in the world, since most of the knowledge of all beings is subject to forgetting over such a span of time and the abundance of the management of affairs in this world and the Hereafter.

In this is a threat to them that their private conferring is a great sin, so they were forbidden from it, and this includes a warning to whoever joins them.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil) for the clause ﴿then He will inform them of what they did﴾, so "inna" served the function of the causal fa' (as in the verse of Bashshar: "Indeed, that success is in early rising"), and the emphasis of the clause with "inna" is for the sake of attention to it; otherwise the addressee would not hesitate about that. This allusive threat indicates that the prohibition on private conferring preceded the revelation of this verse and the verses after it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 58, Verse 8**

﴿Have you not seen those who were forbidden from secret conferring, then return to what they were forbidden, and confer with one another in sin, transgression, and disobedience to the Messenger?﴾

If this verse and the two verses after it were revealed together with the verse before it, as the apparent order of recitation suggests, then the words ﴿were forbidden from secret conferring﴾ indicate that a prohibition on secret conferring had come before the revelation of these verses. This is the apparent meaning of the statement of Mujahid and Qatadah: they were revealed concerning a group of Jews and hypocrites whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had forbidden from conferring secretly in the presence of the believers, but they did not desist, so these verses were revealed. In that case, the four verses were revealed to rebuke them, and this is what we have adopted above.

If, however, these verses were revealed some time after the verse before them, then the prohibition meant is the one alluded to by the words ﴿Then He will inform them of what they did on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 7], as mentioned earlier. That is, they did not desist from secret conferring after they heard the threat against it in the words ﴿Then He will inform them of what they did on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 7]. Thus, the ones meant by ﴿those who were forbidden from secret conferring﴾ are those referred to in His words ﴿There is no secret conference of three but that He is the fourth of them﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 7], and so on.

The "thumma" (then) in His words ﴿then return﴾ indicates a gradation of rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi, meaning a delay that signifies a greater degree rather than a mere lapse of time), because their returning to secret conferring after being forbidden from it is greater than the beginning of the conferring. The beginning of it was sinful because their conferring included evil intentions toward the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims. As for their returning to it after being forbidden, they added to it defiance of the Prophet (ﷺ) and opposition to the Muslims.

Accordingly, the sentence is a fresh beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i, a new independent statement), necessitated by the continued secret conferring of the hypocrites.

[Page 29]

The interrogative in His words ﴿Have you not seen those who were forbidden from secret conferring﴾ is a wondering question (ta'jibi), intended to rebuke them when they hear it.

The verb "ra'a" (to see) is visual, as indicated by its being construed with the preposition ilā (to).

The definite article in "al-najwa" (the secret conferring) is the definite article of prior reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), because the context of the speech concerns a specific kind of secret conferring: the kind that grieves those who believe, as His words indicate: ﴿Secret conferring is only from Satan, to grieve those who believe﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 10].

It is possible that the prohibition, at the beginning, concerned the category of secret conferring in general, covering every conference in view of people, as a means of blocking the pretext (sadd al-dhari'ah, preventing what may lead to harm). Al-Baji said in al-Muntaqa: It is narrated that the prohibition on conferring between two or more, to the exclusion of one, was at the beginning of Islam, and when Islam spread and people believed, this ruling ceased because its cause had ceased.

Ibn al-'Arabi said in Ahkam al-Qur'an, at His words ﴿There is no good in much of their secret conferring﴾ [al-Nisa': 114], in Surah al-Nisa': Allah the Exalted commanded His servants with two great matters. One is sincerity (ikhlas), which is that a person's outward and inward state be equal. The second is giving counsel (nasihah) to the Book of Allah, to His Messenger, to the leaders of the Muslims, and to their common folk. Secret conferring is contrary to these two principles. Given this, people could not avoid having a matter that they share among themselves and that some of them share with others, so this was permitted in the form of enjoining what is good, giving charity, and reconciling between people. End of quotation.

In al-Muwatta' there is a hadith that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When there are three, two should not confer secretly to the exclusion of the third." In a narration of Muslim he added: "Unless with his permission, for that grieves him."

Scholars differed about whether this prohibition is to be understood as prohibition (tahrim) or disapproval (karahah). The majority of the Malikis hold that it is for prohibition. Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-Qabas: If the words "lest it grieve him" come from the Prophet's (ﷺ) statement, then the interpretation is settled; and if they come from the words of the narrator, then it is preferable to another interpretation. Ibn Qasim said: I heard Malik say: Four should not confer secretly to the exclusion of one. As for a group conferring to the exclusion of another group, it is also disliked or forbidden. End of quotation. Al-Nawawi reported a consensus (ijma') on the permissibility of a group conferring to the exclusion of another group, and Ibn al-Tin argued for it with the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I came to him, meaning the Prophet (ﷺ), while he was in a gathering, and I whispered to him." The hadith of 'A'ishah concerning the story of Fatimah also indicates permissibility.

[Page 30]

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: It is not permissible for anyone to enter upon two people who are conferring while they are conferring.

Attached to secret conferring is that two men speak in a language that a third person with them does not understand.

The discussion of the use of His words ﴿then return to what they were forbidden﴾ in its figurative meaning, and of its construction with the preposition li- (to/for), is analogous to the discussion of His words ﴿then return to what they said﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 3].

The same applies to the position of "thumma" (then) as a conjunction of the sentence.

The imperfect form in "ya'udun" (they return) indicates recurrence, that is, they repeat the act to such a degree that they intend thereby disobedience and little concern for the prohibition. For if they returned to secret conferring once or twice, their situation could be that they had forgotten.

What they were forbidden from is the secret conferring. He departed from using a pronoun referring to "secret conferring" and instead used the relative pronoun with its clause (al-ism al-mawsul wa silatuh), because of what the clause indicates of the reason for what follows of the threat in His words ﴿Hell is sufficient for them﴾, along with what the clause contains of recording their foolishness.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read ﴿yatanajawna﴾ (they confer secretly) in the form of tafa'ul from najā in its augmented form. Hamzah, Ruways, and Ya'qub read ﴿yantajūna﴾ in the form of if'ilal from the unaugmented triliteral najā, meaning he whispered to another. The if'ilal form may also carry the meaning of mufa'alah (mutual action), like ikhtasamu (they quarrelled) and iqtatalu (they fought).

"Al-ithm" (sin) is disobedience, and it is what their secret conferring includes of words of disbelief and disparagement of the Muslims.

"Al-'udwan" (transgression), with a ḍammah on the 'ayn, is injustice, and it is what they plot of schemes against the Muslims.

"Ma'siyat al-Rasul" (disobedience to the Messenger) is opposing what he commands them, and among that is that he forbade them from secret conferring and they return to it.

The bāʾ in ﴿with sin﴾ indicates accompaniment (al-mula'abah), meaning they confer while being associated with sin, transgression, and disobedience to the Messenger. This accompaniment varies. The association with sin and transgression is the association of the one conferring in relation to the matter concerning the action of the conferrers. The association with disobedience to the Messenger (ﷺ) is the association of concomitance with the action, because their conferring after the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade them from it is disobedience. In His words ﴿forbidden from secret conferring﴾ and His words ﴿and disobedience to the Messenger﴾ there is evidence that they are hypocrites and not Jews, because the Prophet (ﷺ) did not forbid the Jews from their affairs. This refutes the view of those who interpreted the verse as referring to the Jews, which is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah. Rather, the truth is what is in Ibn 'Atiyyah from Ibn 'Abbas, that it was revealed concerning the hypocrites.

* * *

﴿And when they come to you, they greet you with that by which Allah has not greeted you, and they say to themselves, "Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?" Hell is sufficient for them; they will burn therein, and wretched is the destination.﴾

After mentioning their situation in withdrawing with one another, he mentions the state of their wicked intentions when present in the gathering of the Prophet (ﷺ). They seek out evil intentions through words that outwardly appear to the listeners to be proper. So when they entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ), they would mumble the phrase "as-salamu 'alaykum" (peace be upon you), because it is the emblem of Islam and because of its meaning of gathering safety. They would avoid it and say "An'im sabahan" (may you have a pleasant morning), which was the greeting of the Arabs in the pre-Islamic period, for they did not like to abandon the customs of the Jahiliyyah. Ibn 'Atiyyah reported this from Ibn 'Abbas.

So the meaning of ﴿with that by which Allah has not greeted you﴾ is: without the word of peace, for Allah greeted him with it specifically in His words ﴿O you who have believed, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56]. He greeted him with it among the prophets in general in His words ﴿Say: "Praise be to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen"﴾ [al-Naml: 59]. The greeting of Allah is the complete greeting.

The meaning of this verse is not what is narrated in the hadith that the Jews, when they greeted the Prophet (ﷺ), would say "as-sam 'alayka" (death upon you), and the Prophet (ﷺ) would reply to them, "wa 'alaykum" (and upon you). For that is recorded concerning a people known to be Jews. What is mentioned at the beginning of this verse cannot fittingly be understood as referring to the conditions of the Jews, as you have learned above. And if the pronoun in "jā'ūka" (they came to you) were understood as referring to the Jews, it would necessitate the scattering of the pronouns.

As for this verse, it concerns the conditions of the hypocrites. This is similar to what some of them said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Ra'ina" (our shepherd, i.e., attend to us), which they had learned from the Jews, while they intended a meaning of ra'ana (foolish talk) by it. So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not say "Ra'ina" but say "Unzurna" and listen. And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Baqarah: 104]. And He did not intend by it the prohibition of the Jews.

The meaning of "yaqulūna fī anfusihim" (they say to themselves) is that some of them say to others, in the manner of His words ﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another﴾ [al-Nur: 61], and His words ﴿The believing men and believing women thought well of one another﴾ [al-Nur: 12], meaning some of them thought well of others, that is, some say to others.

It is also possible that what is meant by "anfusihim" (themselves) is their inner assemblies, as in His words ﴿And say to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 63], meaning: speak to them privately, concealing them from exposure. This was discussed in Surah al-Nisa'.

"Lawla" (why not) here is for urging (li al-tahdid), meaning: why does Allah not punish us for the words we exchange privately, in disparaging the Prophet (ﷺ) and similar things? That is, they say something whose meaning is: If Muhammad were a prophet, Allah would have punished us for what we say of evil and blame concerning him. This is what Allah summarized from their words with the expression ﴿Why does Allah not punish us﴾. For "lawla" used for urging is here a metonymy (kinayah) for the denial of the Prophet's (ﷺ) prophethood, meaning: If he were a prophet, Allah would have been angry with us and would now punish us for our saying this to him.

This is one of the notions of the people of misguidance, deeply rooted in them. It is their delusion that the affair of Allah the Exalted is like the affair of humans in hastening vengeance, being shaken by what He does not approve of, and in obstinacy. In a hadith: "No one is more patient with harm he hears than Allah; they ascribe a rival to Him, while He provides for them." Moreover, because of their denial of resurrection and recompense, they reckon that the punishment of Allah the Exalted appears in this world. This is among the delusions. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has destroyed you, and you have become among the losers﴾ [Fussilat: 23]. Therefore, Allah the Exalted said, in response to their words: ﴿Hell is sufficient for them﴾, meaning: Hell is sufficient for them of punishment, for it is a punishment.

The original form of "yaslawnaha" (they will burn therein) is yaslawna bi-ha (they will burn by it), and it has been construed to include the meaning of yadhuqunaha (they will taste it) or yahussunaha (they will feel it). This usage has been repeated in the Qur'an.

His words ﴿and wretched is the destination﴾ are a consequence (tafri') of the threat, in connection with the censure of Hell.

[Page 33]

Address to the hypocrites who display faith. Allah dealt with them according to what they displayed and addressed them with the description of those who believe, as He said: ﴿Among those who say, "We believe," with their mouths, but their hearts have not believed﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 5:41).

Among this usage is what Allah related about the polytheists: ﴿And they say, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are a madman!"﴾ (Al-Hijr 15:6). That means: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down," according to their claim. Allah alerted them to rectify their condition by abandoning the traces of hypocrisy, following the Qur'an's custom of pairing warning with encouragement. So the sentence is a fresh beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i, a new sentence that begins a separate topic).

That is because the hypocrites used to act like the people of faith when they met the believers. But when they returned to their own people, disbelief prevailed over them, so in some of their states they came close to faith because of their mixing with the believers. For this reason Allah struck a parable for them with light, in His saying: ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire, and when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:17), then His saying: ﴿Every time it lights for them, they walk therein, and when darkness falls over them, they stand still﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:20). This is what fits His saying: ﴿so do not confer secretly in sin and aggression and disobedience to the Messenger﴾. His saying ﴿but confer in righteousness and piety﴾ would then be an alert to what is obligatory for them if they must hold private consultations.

It is also permissible that the address is to sincere believers, Allah directing the address to them to teach them what is good and what is bad in private conferring, in connection with the censure of the hypocrites' private conferring. Therefore it began with a prohibition of the like of the hypocrites' conferring, even though such a thing does not come from the believers, as an allusion to the hypocrites. This is like His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who disbelieved and said to their brothers when they traveled in the land or were raiders, "Had they been with us, they would not have died or been killed," so that Allah may make that a regret in their hearts﴾ (Ali 'Imran 3:156). In that case the intended purpose of the speech would be His saying ﴿but confer in righteousness and piety﴾, as teaching for the believers.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read ﴿فَلا تَتَناجَوْا﴾ in the form of tafa'ala (the verbal pattern expressing mutual action). Ruways, from Ya'qub, alone read it as (فَلا تَنْتَجُوا), on the pattern of تَنْتَهُوا.

The imperative in His saying ﴿وتَناجَوْا بِالبِرِّ﴾ is used to express permission (ibahah, the grant of permission rather than obligation), as indicated by His saying ﴿when you confer privately﴾.

Sin, aggression, and disobedience to the Messenger have been discussed previously. As for righteousness (al-birr), it is the opposite of sin and aggression, and it encompasses all acts of good that are commanded in the religion.

Taqwa (God-consciousness) means compliance (imtithal, carrying out the commands). It was discussed earlier in His saying ﴿guidance for the God-conscious﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:2) in Surat al-Baqarah.

His saying ﴿to Whom you will be gathered﴾ is a reminder of the Day of Recompense. The meaning is: He to Whom you will be gathered, who will then recompense you.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 58, verse 10:

﴿Secret consultation is only from Satan, to grieve those who believe; yet it harms them not at all, except by the permission of Allah. And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾

This is a consolation for the believers and a reassurance to their souls, by which is removed the grief that befalls them from witnessing the secret consultations of the hypocrites, because their souls' inclinations differ. When they see those who confer secretly, they imagine many suspicions and fears, as has already been mentioned. Thus the sentence is an independent new statement (istinaf ibtida'i, a resumptive sentence beginning a new topic), required by the context of the prohibition on secret consultation. It may also be an explanation (ta'lil) that reinforces the prohibition on secret consultation.

The definite article in "al-najwa" (the secret consultation) is the definite article of prior reference (ta'rif al-'ahd, referring to something already known). That is, it refers to the secret consultation of the hypocrites, who confer with one another in sin, enmity, and disobedience to the Messenger (ﷺ).

The restriction implied by "innama" (only) is a restriction qualifying the subject by an attribute (qasr mawsuf 'ala sifah). The preposition "min" is for origin (ibtida'iyyah). That is, it restricts secret consultation to being from Satan, meaning that it originates from him, because the aims for which they confer secretly are among the greatest of what Satan whispers to the people of misguidance, so that they may do it in order to grieve those who believe, by the thoughts of evil that reach them through the secret consultation. This cause is not a condition of the restriction, for Satan has other causes, such as casting those who confer secretly into error, enlisting them to spread sedition, and other satanic aims.

This cause was singled out for mention because the purpose is to console the believers and to make them patient under the harm of the hypocrites. For this reason it is followed by His saying ﴿and it harms them not at all﴾, so that the believers may be reassured by Allah's protection of them from the harm of Satan. This is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ [al-Hijr: 42].

[Page 35]

Nafi' alone read "liyuhzina" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy, so that "alladhina amanu" (those who believe) is the object. The rest read it with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the zāy, as the imperfect of hazina (to grieve), so that "alladhina amanu" is the subject. Both are dialectal forms (lughatan).

The clause ﴿and it harms them not at all﴾ and so on is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah).

The concealed pronoun of the nominative in His saying "bi-darrihim" (harming them) refers back to Satan.

The meaning is that Satan does not harm the believers through secret consultation beyond causing them grief. This is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They will not harm you except with some injury﴾ [Al 'Imran: 111]. Or the pronoun refers back to secret consultation, by interpreting it as the act of conferring secretly, so that the meaning is: the conferring is not harmful to the believers, because most of it arises from imagining that what they fear will happen in the battles.

According to both interpretations, the exception in His saying "illa bi-idhni Allah" (except by the permission of Allah) is an exception from circumstances (istithna' min ahwal). The "ba'" is causal (sababiyyah), meaning: except in the circumstance that Allah has decreed some measure of harm, such as defeat or killing. The "idhn" (permission) here means the command of creation (amr al-takwin).

"Shay'an" (anything) is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), meaning: any measure of harm.

The occurrence of "shay'an" in the context of negation indicates the generality of the negation of every harm from Satan, meaning that every kind of harm from Satan is removed from the believers. This includes the harm of secret consultation and the harm of other things. The exception in His saying "illa bi-idhni Allah" is from the generality of "shay'an" in the context of negation, meaning: no harm that coincides with Allah's permission for Satan to impose his harm upon them through it, that is, the harm of his whispering.

The word "idhn" is borrowed for what Allah placed in the original creation of human nature, namely the influence of souls by what Satan makes attractive to them. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the misguided﴾ [al-Hijr: 42]. So when Allah leaves room between the whispering and the servant, the servant draws near to visible and hidden sins in every state in which the believer turns away from observing the commands and prohibitions of the Law. This harm is what is expressed by "sultan" (authority) in His saying, exalted is He, concerning Satan, ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the misguided﴾ [al-Hijr: 42], meaning: you have authority over them. These divine dispositions proceed according to the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, and according to what He knows of His servants' words and inner secrets, and He knows the secret and what is more hidden.

[Page 36]

For this reason it is concluded with His saying ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾, because when they rely upon Allah truly, by exhausting their effort in guarding against the plots of Satan and seeking Allah's help in facilitating that for them, then Allah protects them from the plots of Satan. He, exalted is He, said ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, He is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 3].

It is also possible that the generality of "shay'an" is intended as particular, meaning: it does not harm them with anything of what the secret consultation of the hypocrites suggests to them, such as defeat or killing, except by Allah's decree that a defeat or killing occur.

The meaning is that secret consultation suggests to those who believe what is not actually happening, so Allah informed them that they should not grieve over secret consultation, because affairs proceed according to what Allah has decreed, by the very command of His will, until true reports reach them.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾ is for emphasis on the meaning of this complement.

[Page 37]

﴿O you who believe, when it is said to you, "Make room in the assemblies," then make room; Allah will make room for you. And when it is said, "Rise up," then rise up; Allah will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge by degrees. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

He separated the verses on the rules of private consultation (najwa) from this verse, in consideration of the unity of subject between the meaning of this verse and the meaning of the one that follows it, in that both are united by the aim of showing proper conduct toward the Messenger (ﷺ). This consideration is preferable to considering the unity of the context of the rulings.

So in this verse there is an instruction in conduct in the assembly of the Messenger (ﷺ), and the verse that follows it concerns proper conduct in confidential speech with the Messenger (ﷺ). He placed that (second) verse apart from the verses on general consultation, to signal its excellence over the consultation contained in the preceding verses. Thus the unity of the category of consultation is what justifies the transition from the first type to the second type, and the indication of its distinction by excellence is what required separating the two types with the verse on the conduct of the Prophetic assembly.

Also, the hypocrites had an intention of deception concerning the matter of the assembly, just as they had an intention of deception in the consultation. This is what created the occasion for the transition from speaking about consultation to mentioning making room in the noble Prophetic assembly.

[Page 38]

It is narrated from Muqatil that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was in the Suffah (the shaded area of the mosque where the poor Companions stayed), and there was crowding in the place on a Friday. Some people from among the people of Badr came, among them Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, and they had arrived earlier at the assembly, so they stood on their feet waiting for room to be made for them. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to honour the people of Badr, so he said to those around him: 'Stand up, so-and-so, in the number of those standing from the people of Badr.' This displeased those who had been made to stand, and the hypocrites winked and said: 'These people have not been treated fairly, for they loved to be near their Prophet, so they got to his assembly first.' So Allah revealed this verse." This was to console the hearts of those who had been made to stand, and to teach the Ummah the obligation of honouring the excellence of those of excellence among them, and the obligation of acknowledging the merit of people of merit. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not wish for that by which Allah has favoured some of you over others﴾ [al-Nisa: 32], and He said: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest. Those are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterwards. But to all Allah has promised the best﴾ [al-Hadid: 10].

The address with "O you who believe" is an address to all the believers, encompassing those who were present in the assembly in which the occasion of revelation took place, and others who might attend the assembly of the Messenger (ﷺ).

The verse begins with the command to make room, because the standing of those who were made to stand was only for the purpose of making room. So attaching the ruling to this is an indication of the effective cause (ʿillah) of the ruling.

Al-tafassuh (making room) means expansion. It is a form from fasaḥa lahu (with the sīn lightly pronounced) when one creates a space for him in a place; and fasuha al-makan (with the verb of the pattern karuma) means the place became spacious. The form tafaʿʿul here implies exertion, i.e., one is required to make a space, and this involves squeezing together with those sitting.

The definiteness of "the assembly" (al-majlis) may be the definiteness of prior reference, namely the assembly of the Prophet (ﷺ), i.e., if the Prophet (ﷺ) says that to you, because his command is only for the sake of observing a superior right of another. The majlis is the place of sitting. The assembly of the Prophet (ﷺ) was in his mosque, and most often his sitting place was that called al-Rawdah, which is the area between the Prophet's (ﷺ) minbar and his house.

It may also be that the definiteness of "the assembly" is the definiteness of the genus. The words ﴿Allah will make room for you﴾

[Page 39]

are in the jussive mood as the answer to his words "make room" (fafsaḥū). This is a promise of reward for obeying the command to make room, of the same kind as the action, since Allah's giving room to the one who obeys is made a recompense for his obedience, which is making room for others. So the pronoun in "for you" refers to those who believe, on the basis that those who make room are among the believers, since the ruling is common to the whole community, and the reward is specifically for those upon whom the command falls in a binding way.

The complement of ﴿Allah will make room for you﴾ is omitted so that it covers everything for which people seek room, in its literal and figurative senses, in this world and the Hereafter: place, provision, or a Garden whose breadth is the heavens and the earth, according to intentions. Its specification is left to the will of Allah the Exalted.

The subject of the saying is omitted because it is obvious, meaning: if the Messenger says to you, "Make room," then make room, for Allah will reward you for that.

So the verse indicates only the command to make room when the Prophet (ﷺ) commands it. But from it is derived that the believers making room for one another in assemblies is praiseworthy and commanded, either obligatorily or recommendedly, since it is part of generosity and kindness. It is therefore among the things that complete the obligation of mutual love among Muslims, even if there is hardship for the owner of the spot, when another squeezes him there. That hardship is not considered when weighed against the benefit of love and its fruits, provided it does not lead to severe crowding and harm, or to the loss of a benefit such as hearing (a lecture) or the like, like the assemblies of knowledge and hadith and the rows of prayer. This is analogy based on the assembly of the Prophet (ﷺ), in that it is an assembly of goodness. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The most beloved of you to me are those among you who are gentlest in shoulders during prayer." Malik said: "I do not see the ruling but as applying generally in assemblies of knowledge and the like, forever." He means that this ruling, though it was revealed concerning the assembly of the Prophet (ﷺ), is inclusive of the assemblies of the Muslims that are assemblies of goodness, because this is conduct and solidarity. There is no indication of its being specific to the Prophetic assemblies. By "the like" (nahwuhā) Malik meant every assembly in which there is an important matter concerning the affairs of religion, for it is the right of Muslims to be eager to help one another attend it. This is analogy on the assembly of the Prophet (ﷺ), and its effective cause is cooperation in public interests.

The word "making room" implies avoiding crowding and tight packing such that the purpose of attending that assembly is lost, or pain is caused to those sitting.

[Page 40]

Malik allowed one to skip the invitation to a wedding feast if the crowding there is great.

The majority read "fī al-majlis" (in the assembly, singular), and ʿĀṣim read it in the plural form ﴿fī al-majālis﴾ (in the assemblies). On both readings it is possible that the article (al-) is for prior reference or for the genus, and that the intended meaning is the assemblies of the Prophet (ﷺ) whenever they recur, or whatever includes all the assemblies of Muslims. On both readings the command in His words "then make room" (fafsaḥū) is valid as obligatory or recommended.

His words ﴿And when it is said, "Rise up," then rise up﴾ and what follows are a conjunction on ﴿when it is said to you, "Make room in the assemblies"﴾.

"Unshuzū" (rise up) is a command from nasha, meaning to rise from one's place. It is said: nasha yanshuzu (of the pattern qaʿada and ḍaraba), meaning to be raised, because standing up is a rising from the place where one has settled. The rebellion (nushūz) of a wife against her husband is used figuratively for her staying away from his bed. Nushūz is more specific than tafassuh in one respect, so it is a conjunction of what is more specific in one respect onto what is more general, for the sake of giving importance to the conjoined element, since standing up from the assembly is stronger than making room while seated. So nushūz was mentioned lest it be thought that the commanded making room is making room while seated, especially since the occasion of revelation involved standing up, and this is the intended matter from the revelation of the verse according to that report. Some of the exegetes explained nushūz as standing up from the assembly of the Messenger (ﷺ) in general, whether for making room or for other reasons for which one is commanded to stand. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, and al-Hasan: "When it is said, 'Rise up,' (rise up) toward goodness and toward prayer."

Ibn Zayd said: "When it is said, 'Rise up' from the house of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then go up, for the Prophet (ﷺ) has needs. When they were in his house, each one of them loved that his last contact be with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The occasion of revelation does not restrict the general or limit the absolute.

This ruling applies when making room is difficult and the crowding and packing is severe. Then those who occupy seats have the established right to continue sitting, and no one is made to stand for another. This is so when the one for whose sake someone is made to stand has more right to the place than the one who is made to stand, by some cause of priority, as the Prophet (ﷺ) did when he had some men stand so that their seats could be given to the people of Badr. From this is the priority of students of knowledge in the sessions of lessons, and the priority of people in the seats of mosques by precedence and the like. If no one has priority over another, then the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade that a man be made to rise from his assembly and then sit in it himself.

[Page 41]

A man may send his prayer mat, rug, or carpet to the mosque, to be spread for him in a place of the mosque until he comes and sits on it, for that is claiming that place at that time. Ibn Sirin used to send his servant to the mosque on Friday, and he would sit there for him; when Ibn Sirin came, the servant would rise from it for him.

In the Muwatta' (of Malik), from Malik ibn Abi ʿAmir, who said: "I used to see a carpet belonging to ʿAqil ibn Abi Talib being put down on Friday against the western wall of the mosque; when the carpet's entire area was covered by the shade of the wall, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab came out and led the Friday prayer." So the carpet and the like is the claiming of the place for the owner of the rug.

So one may order someone who gets up early to go to the mosque and take a place to sit in until the one who sent him arrives, and then he leaves the spot for him, because this is of the category of acting as a deputy in claiming a right.

Ibn Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, ʿĀṣim, and Abu Jaʿfar read ﴿unshuzū fa-unshuzū﴾ with a ḍammah on the shīn in both places. The rest read it with a kasrah on the shīn. They are two dialects for the imperfect of nasha.

His words ﴿Allah will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge by degrees﴾ are the answer to the command in His words "then rise up" (fa-unshuzū). The reciters have agreed on the jussive of the verb yarfaʿu, so it is the answer of the command by this. He promised reward for obeying the legal command in what contains a command, or for what the command implies of a cause by which the like of the one commanded is measured, of what contains the effective cause of the ruling, as was mentioned in His words "then make room" (fafsaḥū).

Since nushūz is a rising from the place where one was, its reward is of the same kind.

The indefiniteness of "degrees" (darajāt) is to indicate its kinds, of the degrees of this world and degrees of the Hereafter.

The pronoun in "of you" is an address to those who were called with "O you who believe."

The min (of) in "of you" is partitive, meaning: Allah will raise the degrees of those who obeyed. The indication of this interpretation is that the verb is made a reward for the command, since the reward is caused by what is ordered by it. His words "of you" describe "those who believe," meaning: those who believe from among the believers. The difference between the sense of the description and the sense of the described is by the difference of what is implied, even if the words of the description and the described are synonymous outwardly. So the sentence comes to the implied meaning: Allah will raise those who responded to the command to rise up when they are among the believers, that is, not those among the hypocrites whom the assembly includes.

[Page 42]

So the apparent requirement would be to say, "Allah will raise those of you who rise up," but the relative clause is brought in with the connection of faith, because of what the connection indicates of the cause of the raising of degrees, namely their obedience to the command of the one who said "rise up," who is the Messenger (ﷺ), if it is due to their faith; and that this obedience comes from their faith, not from hypocrisy, nor from resentment on the part of its doer.

He conjoined "those who have been given knowledge among you" as a conjunction of the particular onto the general, because attending the assembly of the Messenger (ﷺ) is only for seeking knowledge from his admonitions and teaching. That is, "and those who have been given knowledge among you, O believers," because it may be that the command for someone to rise from the assembly is for their sake, i.e., for the sake of seating them. That is a raising of their degrees in this world. Also, when they are able to be in the assembly of the Messenger (ﷺ), their being settled is more complete for understanding and more removing of boredom; this is more conducive to lengthening their sitting and increasing their receiving, and to abundance of the deductions of their understanding in what is conveyed to them of knowledge. So the making of those sitting rise in the assembly for the sake of seating those who have been given knowledge is a raising of their degrees in this world.

Perhaps the Badris, whose case the verse was revealed about, were among the Companions who were given knowledge.

It is also possible that some of those who were ordered to stand were among the people of knowledge, and he was made to stand up for the sake of the superiority of the Badris over him. Then in the promise to the one who was made to rise from his place, with raising of ranks, there is a comfort for him, that Allah is the one who raises his rank.

This is the interpretation of the structure of the verse that the strength of its concision requires. The commentators have gone in many directions in clarifying the meaning derived from this wondrous structure, but what we have followed is clearer than them.

"Darajat" (ranks) is in the accusative as an adverb of place, related to "yarfa'" (He will raise), meaning: Allah will raise those who believe with a raising that exists in ranks.

It is also possible that it serves as a substitute for the absolute object of "yarfa'," since these are ranks of raising, i.e., elevations.

The word "darajat" is used metaphorically for honour, for the place of raising in the verse carries a figurative raising, which is preference and honour. The metaphor is supported (tarshih) by describing the raising as "ranks." This supporting description is itself also a metaphor, similar to the supporting description in the words of the Exalted ﴿They break the covenant of Allah after its ratification﴾ [al-Baqarah: 27], and this is the finest kind of tarshih. Its parallel has already been mentioned in the words of the Exalted in Surah al-An'am ﴿We raise in ranks whom We will﴾ [al-An'am: 83].

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and a group of the people of tafsir said: the words ﴿and those who were given knowledge, in ranks﴾ are a new independent statement, and the speech is complete at His words "from among you." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is in the accusative by a hidden verb, and perhaps he means: the accusative of "darajat" is by a verb which is the predicate of the subject, and the estimate is: "He made them (ja'alahum)."

The sentence ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil), meaning: Allah is All-Knowing of your deeds and the varied intentions behind your obedience, like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "No one who is wounded in the way of Allah..." and Allah knows best who is wounded in His way, [the hadith].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 58, verse 12:

﴿O you who have believed, when you consult the Messenger, precede your consultation with a charity. That is better for you and purer. But if you do not find [anything to give], then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

This is a new, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), by which he returns to mention some of the states of private consultation (najwa), and this is one of its praiseworthy states. The connection (munasaba) is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And consult together in righteousness and piety﴾ [al-Mujadila: 9]. This charity was legislated by Allah, exalted is He, and He made its cause the consultation of the Messenger ﷺ. It is mentioned right after the verses on private consultation in order to cover all kinds of consultation, both praiseworthy and blameworthy. The earlier scholars differed about the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse and the wisdom behind legislating the charity of consultation (sadaqat al-munaja). Various reports with differing content have been transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Jabir ibn Zayd, Zayd ibn Aslam and Muqatil concerning its occasion of revelation, and I do not think they intend by them anything other than relating states of consultation that were widespread; when the ruling on the charity of consultation was revealed, people reduced their private consultation. The expressions of the earlier scholars proceeded with leniency, so they would apply the name "occasions of revelation" to examples of rulings and particular instances of general principles, as we have mentioned in the Fifth Introduction of this commentary. Mujahid refrained and did not mention a cause for this verse, confining himself to saying: "They were forbidden from consulting the Messenger until they gave charity."

Page 43
What appears to me is that Allah legislated this charity and made it obligatory upon those who find something to give in charity before consulting the Messenger ﷺ, and He removed it from those who do not find anything to give. Its cause and its time was the time of their turning to consult the Messenger ﷺ. The Muslims were eager to ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about matters of religion every day, so Allah legislated for them this charity every day, for the daily benefit of the poor. The poor at that time were numerous in Medina, among them the People of the Bench (ahl al-Suffa) and most of the Emigrants (muhajirun) who had been expelled from their homes and their wealth.
The more apparent view is that this charity was legislated after the zakat, so it serves the wisdom of enriching the poor day by day, because zakat is paid at the beginning of years and at specific seasons, so what reaches the poor from it may be exhausted before the next zakat period arrives.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the charity of consultation was legislated before the legislation of zakat and was abrogated by the obligation of zakat. The apparent sense of His saying in the following verse, ﴿So establish prayer and give zakat﴾ [al-Mujadila: 13], is that zakat at that time was a separate, known legislation. Perhaps what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, if it is authentically from him, means that it was abrogated by the sufficiency of zakat.

Reports of differing chains have multiplied indicating that this verse was not practiced for long, it being said: ten days. It is reported from al-Kalbi who said: it lasted an hour of a day. That is, it was not practiced for long if the command is meant as obligation; otherwise, the recommendation of this did not cease during the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ, so that the soul of the believer would be purer when meeting the Prophet, similar to the recommendation of renewing wudu for each prayer.

The words of the earlier scholars concur that the ruling of the command in His saying ﴿precede your consultation with a charity﴾ has been abrogated by His saying ﴿So when you did not, and Allah forgave you﴾ [al-Mujadila: 13], and so on. This indicates that the command in it is for obligation. In the tafsir of al-Qurtubi and Ahkam ibn al-Faras there is a relating of statements about the occasion of revelation of this verse that revolve around the idea that this charity was legislated to deter types of people from consulting the Prophet ﷺ, since they had persisted excessively in consulting him without a reason prompting them; the scholar's breast is not at ease with these, due to their weakness in chain and meaning and their contradiction of the objective of the Sharia. The closest of what has been reported about the report of the affirmation of this charity is what is in the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi: "From 'Ali ibn 'Alqama al-Anmari, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: When the verse ﴿O you who have believed, when you consult the Messenger, precede your consultation with a charity﴾ was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ said to me: 'What do you think, a dinar?' I said: 'They cannot bear it.' He said: 'Half a dinar?' I said: 'They cannot bear it.' He said: 'How much then?' I said: 'A barleycorn.' Al-Tirmidhi said: that is, the weight of a barleycorn of gold. He said: 'You are indeed frugal.' So there was revealed ﴿Are you apprehensive that you should precede your consultation with charities?﴾ [al-Mujadila: 13], and so on. He said: 'Through me Allah lightened this for this community.'" Al-Tirmidhi said: this is a hasan gharib hadith, and we only know it through this route.

I say: 'Ali ibn 'Alqama al-Anmari, al-Bukhari said: there is some concern about his hadith, and Ibn Hibban regarded him as trustworthy. Ibn al-Faras said: they have authenticated from 'Ali that he said: no one acted upon it except me. And he cited a hadith.

The meaning of 'Ali's statement "through me Allah lightened this for this community" is that he intended the lightening in the amount of the charity from a dinar to the weight of a barleycorn of gold, which is one of seventy-two parts of a dinar.

The verb najaytum ("you consulted") is used to mean the intention of the act, like His saying ﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 6], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾ [al-Nahl: 98].

The indicator (qarina) is His saying ﴿precede your consultation with a charity﴾.

The majority hold that the command in His saying "fa-qaddimu" (precede) is for obligation; al-Fakhr chose this and preferred it on the basis that it is the default in the form of the imperative, and on His saying ﴿But if you do not find, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, for that is not said except regarding something whose obligation is removed by its absence. It is fitting that this is the view of those who say that this charity was abrogated by the obligation of zakat, and this is from Ibn 'Abbas. A group said: the command is for recommendation (nadb), and this fits the view of those who say that the obligation of zakat preceded the revelation of this verse, for the legislation of zakat nullified every right that was obligatory upon wealth.

And "bayna yadayi najwakum" means: a little before your consultation. It is a metaphorical figure of speech (isti'ara tamthiliyya) that functioned as a proverbial expression for the nearness of a thing shortly before reaching it. It likens the condition of a thing's nearness to another to the condition of a person arriving before someone he is about to approach, a likening of an intellectual image to a sensory one.

Page 45
It is used for nearness in time by likening time to place, as here, and it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾ [al-Baqara: 255]. This has been discussed in Surat al-Baqara.

The reference in ﴿That is better for you﴾ is to the precedence understood from "qaddimu," in the manner of His saying ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 8].

His saying ﴿That is better for you and purer﴾ is a clarification of the wisdom of the command to give charity before the consultation of the Messenger ﷺ, so that those who are inclined would be eager for it.

"Khayr" (better) may be an elative noun (ism tafdil), its original form being akhyar, and it is the one that pairs with "wa-athar" (and purer), meaning: that is more greatly better for you than consulting the Messenger ﷺ without giving charity, although there is good in each. Like His saying: ﴿And if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 271].

It may also be a noun on the pattern (fa'l), the opposite of evil, meaning: precedence of charity before consultation contains good for you, namely attaining the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, at the time of your turning to His Messenger ﷺ, so there is gained from the benefit of consultation what is not gained in its like without precedence of charity.

As for "athar" (purer), it is undoubtedly an elative noun, meaning purer for you, that is, more pure. The purity here is spiritual, namely purity and growth of the soul, because the one who gives charity receives divine lights from the pleasure of Allah with him, so his soul becomes pure, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You purify them and cause them to grow by it﴾ [al-Tawba: 103]. From this, charity was called zakat.

The description of this charity is that it was given to the poor at the time when the Muslim set out to go to the Prophet ﷺ to consult him.

Allah excused those unable to precede with charity by His saying ﴿But if you do not find, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: if you do not find what you may give in charity before the consultation, Allah forgives you the forgiveness that would have been yours had you given charity, because whoever intends to do good, if he were able to do it, has a reward for his intention.

As for deriving that one who does not find [charity] bears no blame for consulting without charity, it is obtained by implication (dalalat al-fahwa), because he does not abandon consulting the Messenger ﷺ; for the desire to consult the Messenger ﷺ is not in vain, but rather to acquire knowledge of matters of religion.

As for His saying "Raheem" (Merciful), it stands in contrast to what the one who does not find [charity] missed of the purification of the soul through giving, indicating that Allah's mercy benefits him.

The scholars agreed that the ruling of this verse is abrogated.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 58, verse 13:

﴿Are you apprehensive that you should offer charity before your private consultation? So if you do not, and Allah has forgiven you, then establish prayer, give zakah, and obey Allah and His Messenger. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ This verse was revealed immediately after the one before it. It is the well-known view of a group of the early exegetes (salaf al-mufassirin) that it was revealed ten days after the preceding one. The reason is that some of the Muslims who were able to give charity before private consultation (najwa) found this difficult, so they refrained from privately consulting the Prophet ﷺ. Then Allah dropped the obligation of this charity. It has been said that no one acted upon this verse except 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. Perhaps others did not need to consult the Messenger ﷺ, and they limited their consultation to what was necessary for the slightest reason.

The address is therefore to a group of believers who were able to give charity before consultation, and it was difficult or burdensome for them.

Al-ishfaq (apprehension) is the expectation of the occurrence of what one does not desire, and the object of ﴿أأشْفَقْتُمْ﴾ is "an tuqaddimu," meaning "from offering," i.e., are you apprehensive of the consequence of that, which is poverty.

The exegetes said that this verse abrogates the one before it (naskh), so the obligation of offering charity for one who wishes to consult the Messenger ﷺ fell away. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, but Ibn 'Atiyyah considered it unlikely.

The interrogation is used to rebuke for reluctance toward that charity, despite its many benefits for the benefit of the poor.

Page 47

Then Allah overlooked it out of mercy toward them, by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So if you do not, and Allah has forgiven you, then establish prayer and give zakah﴾, and so on. It is known from the reproachful interrogation that some of them did not do that.

The particle (idh) is temporal, implying causation, i.e., "since you did not do it, then establish prayer."

The fa' in ﴿فَإذْ لَمْ تَفْعَلُوا﴾ serves to make what follows a consequence of the reproachful interrogation.

The clause ﴿وتابَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah), and the waw is parenthetical. What "idh" depends upon is omitted, indicated by His saying ﴿وتابَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾; its estimated meaning is: "We have lightened it for you and excused you from offering charity before consulting the Messenger ﷺ." The fa' in "fa-aqimu al-salah" is coordinating with the omitted speech, and "hafizu" (maintain) the other obligations: establishing prayer, giving zakah, and obeying Allah and His Messenger. That is, there is no leniency in these matters. It was said to them this so that they would not assume that whenever carrying out what they were charged with became burdensome, they would be excused from it.

Since zakah, as an obligation, preceded the command regarding the charity of consultation according to the more correct view, the verb "atawa" (give) is used to denote continuity, like the verb "fa-aqimu."

Know that the fa' often occurs after "idh" and its complement, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿وإذْ لَمْ يَهْتَدُوا بِهِ فَسَيَقُولُونَ هَذا إفْكٌ قَدِيمٌ﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 11] in Surah al-Ahqaf, and ﴿وإذِ اعْتَزَلْتُمُوهم وما يَعْبُدُونَ إلّا اللَّهَ فَأْوُوا إلى الكَهْفِ﴾ [al-Kahf: 16] in Surah al-Kahf.

The clause ﴿واللَّهُ خَبِيرٌ بِما تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ is a concluding appendage (tadhyil) to the clause ﴿فَأقِيمُوا الصَّلاةَ وآتُوا الزَّكاةَ﴾, and it is a metonymy (kinayah) for warning against negligence in obeying Allah and His Messenger.

[Page 48]

These verses describe another condition of the hypocrites: they take as allies the Jews, even though they are not of the same religious community, since the hypocrites belong to the people of polytheism.

The sentence is a fresh, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i, a new sentence that begins a topic), because it returns to the subject that was introduced by the verses ﴿Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger will be humiliated﴾ [al-Mujadila: 5], after a long digression of many digressive passages.

The people with whom Allah is angry are the Jews, who are known by a description that has the same meaning as this phrase in the Qur'an, in His words ﴿not of those who have earned anger﴾ [al-Fatiha: 7].

The interrogative is expressive of wonder, like His words ﴿Have you not seen those who were forbidden from secret counsel?﴾ [al-Mujadila: 8].

The aspect of wonder regarding their condition is that they took as allies a people who are not of their own kind and who are not of their religion. What drove them to this alliance was nothing but the shared enmity of both groups toward Islam and the Muslims.

The pronoun in ﴿ما هم﴾ (ma hum) may refer back to those who took allies, namely the hypocrites. In that case the clause ﴿ما هم منكم ولا منهم﴾ (ma hum minkum wa la minhum) is a circumstantial clause (hal, a clause describing the state of the subject) modifying "those who took allies," meaning: they are neither Muslims nor Jews. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer back to "a people," namely the Jews, so that the clause ﴿ما هم منكم﴾ becomes a descriptive clause (sifah) of "a people," meaning: a people who are neither Muslims nor polytheists, but rather Jews.

Likewise, the pronoun in ﴿ولا منهم﴾ (wa la minhum) admits both meanings, by reversal. Both possibilities are intended, following the method of directed speech (al-kalam al-muwajjah, speech that can be understood in more than one direction), which multiplies meanings while remaining concise. Thus it conveys wonder at the condition of the hypocrites: that they take as allies a people who are foreign to them, and who are themselves foreign to them. Moreover, if the difference of religion separates them from the Muslims, what separates them from the Jews is both the difference of religion and the difference of lineage, since the hypocrites are Arabs from Yathrib.

According to the other possibility, the statement informs about the hypocrites that their Islam is not sincere, meaning: they are not of you, O Muslims, and this is the intended meaning. On this reading, the phrase ﴿ولا منهم﴾ serves as a precaution (ihtiras, a clause that guards against a misunderstanding) and as a completion (tatmim, a clause that completes the meaning) of the description of their condition. On this reading the censure of the hypocrites is even stronger, because it shows their foolishness: they made as their allies people who are not of their religion, so their alliance cannot be trusted. They also concealed hatred of the Muslims, and so they did not find the true religion.

﴿And they swear falsely﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) with "took allies" and is expressed in the present tense to indicate its recurrence and to bring the strange situation before the mind at the time of their oath, a false oath made to disown what they had done. "Falsehood" (al-kadhib) is a report that contradicts reality, and these are the reports they give about themselves, denying what proceeds from them against the Muslims.

[Page 49]

﴿And they know﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). This adds to the wonder, because it is more shameful than swearing falsely, since it shows a lack of certainty about what is sworn to.

This refers to what the hypocrites used to swear to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to the Muslims whenever some of their schemes were exposed. Among this is the saying of Allah the Exalted about them: ﴿They swear by Allah that they are of you, but they are not of you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 56], His saying ﴿They swear by Allah to you in order to please you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62], and His saying ﴿They swear by Allah that they did not say it, but they had certainly uttered the word of disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74].

Al-Suddi and Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Ubayy and Abdullah ibn Nabtal (with the letter nun, then the letter ba' with one dot, then a letter ta' with two dots above). One of them, namely Abdullah ibn Nabtal, used to sit with the Prophet (ﷺ), and would convey his news to the Jews and revile the Prophet (ﷺ). When the report of this reached him, or when Allah informed him of it, he came and made excuses and swore that he had not done it.

The clause ﴿Indeed they, what evil they used to do﴾ is a reason (ta'lil) for the preparation of the punishment for them. That is, they did evil deeds in the past, lengthy and repeated, as the present tense in His words "they used to do" (ya'malun) indicates.

Between (ya'malun, "they do") and (ya'lamun, "they know") there is an inverted paronomasia (al-jinas al-maqlub, a play on words in which the letters of one word are reversed in the other), where the letters of one word are transposed to form the other.

These verses describe another condition of the hypocrites: they take as allies the Jews, even though they are not of the same religious community, since the hypocrites belong to the people of polytheism.

The sentence is a fresh, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i, a new sentence that begins a topic), because it returns to the subject that was introduced by the verses ﴿Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger will be humiliated﴾ [al-Mujadila: 5], after a long digression of many digressive passages.

The people with whom Allah is angry are the Jews, who are known by a description that has the same meaning as this phrase in the Qur'an, in His words ﴿not of those who have earned anger﴾ [al-Fatiha: 7].

The interrogative is expressive of wonder, like His words ﴿Have you not seen those who were forbidden from secret counsel?﴾ [al-Mujadila: 8].

The aspect of wonder regarding their condition is that they took as allies a people who are not of their own kind and who are not of their religion. What drove them to this alliance was nothing but the shared enmity of both groups toward Islam and the Muslims.

The pronoun in ﴿ما هم﴾ (ma hum) may refer back to those who took allies, namely the hypocrites. In that case the clause ﴿ما هم منكم ولا منهم﴾ (ma hum minkum wa la minhum) is a circumstantial clause (hal, a clause describing the state of the subject) modifying "those who took allies," meaning: they are neither Muslims nor Jews. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer back to "a people," namely the Jews, so that the clause ﴿ما هم منكم﴾ becomes a descriptive clause (sifah) of "a people," meaning: a people who are neither Muslims nor polytheists, but rather Jews.

Likewise, the pronoun in ﴿ولا منهم﴾ (wa la minhum) admits both meanings, by reversal. Both possibilities are intended, following the method of directed speech (al-kalam al-muwajjah, speech that can be understood in more than one direction), which multiplies meanings while remaining concise. Thus it conveys wonder at the condition of the hypocrites: that they take as allies a people who are foreign to them, and who are themselves foreign to them. Moreover, if the difference of religion separates them from the Muslims, what separates them from the Jews is both the difference of religion and the difference of lineage, since the hypocrites are Arabs from Yathrib.

According to the other possibility, the statement informs about the hypocrites that their Islam is not sincere, meaning: they are not of you, O Muslims, and this is the intended meaning. On this reading, the phrase ﴿ولا منهم﴾ serves as a precaution (ihtiras, a clause that guards against a misunderstanding) and as a completion (tatmim, a clause that completes the meaning) of the description of their condition. On this reading the censure of the hypocrites is even stronger, because it shows their foolishness: they made as their allies people who are not of their religion, so their alliance cannot be trusted. They also concealed hatred of the Muslims, and so they did not find the true religion.

﴿And they swear falsely﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) with "took allies" and is expressed in the present tense to indicate its recurrence and to bring the strange situation before the mind at the time of their oath, a false oath made to disown what they had done. "Falsehood" (al-kadhib) is a report that contradicts reality, and these are the reports they give about themselves, denying what proceeds from them against the Muslims.

﴿And they know﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). This adds to the wonder, because it is more shameful than swearing falsely, since it shows a lack of certainty about what is sworn to.

This refers to what the hypocrites used to swear to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to the Muslims whenever some of their schemes were exposed. Among this is the saying of Allah the Exalted about them: ﴿They swear by Allah that they are of you, but they are not of you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 56], His saying ﴿They swear by Allah to you in order to please you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62], and His saying ﴿They swear by Allah that they did not say it, but they had certainly uttered the word of disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74].
