This is a resumed clause (*isti'naf*) that serves as an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*) of the clause ﴿they swear falsely knowingly﴾ [al-Mujadila: 14], because that prompts a questioner to ask what compelled them to swear falsely. The answer is that they did so to accomplish their aims and to increase their deceit. It is also permissible to make the clause a second predicate (*khabar thani*) of *inna* in His saying ﴿Indeed, evil is what they used to do﴾ [al-Mujadila: 15], in which case it falls within the causal explanation (*ta'lil*).

*Al-junnah* means protection and cover, from *janna*, meaning he concealed himself. It is a protection against the Muslims' awareness of them, so that they could prevent many who wish to enter Islam from entering it, because they fabricate falsehoods that they attribute to Islam. This is the meaning of the consequential *fa* (*tafri' bi-l-fa'*) in His saying ﴿so they barred [others] from the way of Allah﴾.

*Saddu* may be transitive, with its object omitted because it is clear, meaning: so they barred people from the way of Allah, that is Islam, by discouraging them and attaching accusations and defects to the religion. It may also be intransitive, meaning: so they themselves turned away from the way of Allah. The use of the past tense *saddu* ʿan sabili Allah, as a consequence of ﴿they took their oaths as a shield﴾, although their oaths occurred after they had barred [others] from the way of Allah, is on both readings intended to reflect the second consequence, which is ﴿so for them is a humiliating punishment﴾.

The consequence ﴿so for them is a humiliating punishment﴾ is stated so that it is known that what they took of their oaths as a shield is a cause among the causes of punishment, one that requires the punishment to be multiplied. He first described the punishment as *shadid* (severe), which is the recompense for their alliance with a people upon whom Allah is wrathful and for their swearing falsely.

He described their punishment a second time as *muhin* (humiliating), because it is a recompense for their barring people from the way of Allah. This is the meaning of "severe in punishment" because of the great magnitude of the crime, as in His saying ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred [others] from the way of Allah, We shall increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾ [al-Nahl: 88].

Thus the punishment was suited to both aspects of their disbelief, and it is one punishment that bears both descriptions. He repeated its mention for the sake of emphasis in warning and threat, since this is a context that calls for repetition, and it is embellished by the variation of the two descriptions.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 58, verse 17:

﴿Their wealth will not avail them, nor their children, against Allah at all. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾ This is related to His saying: ﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾ [al-Mujadila: 16]. Just as their oaths did not shield them from the punishment, their wealth and their helpers will not avail them anything on the Day of Resurrection.

The hypocrites were among the wealthy people of Medina, and their wealth was among the causes of their aversion to accepting Islam, because they were people of leadership (siyada) and they did not wish to become part of the common class (tabaqat 'umum) of people. 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul was prepared to be made king over Medina before the conversion of the Ansar (al-Ansar), so they boasted over the Muslims with abundance of wealth and multitude of clans, and that was in the first year of the Hijra. Among that is the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul: (If we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner therefrom). By "the mightier" he meant his faction, and by "the meaner" he meant the faction of the Muslims. So Allah informed them that their wealth and their children would not avail them against what Allah had threatened them with of humiliation in this world and punishment in the Hereafter. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿If the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease and the agitators in Medina do not cease, We will surely incite you against them; then they will not remain your neighbors therein except for a little, cursed. Wherever they are found, they will be seized and slain with [intense] slaughter﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60]. And if they did not avail them against Allah in this world, then it is more fitting that they would not avail them anything against the punishment of the Hereafter, i.e., not even a little of availing.

And from Muqatil: that they said, "Muhammad claims that he will be victorious on the Day of Resurrection. Woe to us then! By Allah, we will indeed be victorious on the Day of Resurrection with our selves, our children and our wealth, if there is a Resurrection." So this verse was revealed.

The insertion of the negation particle in the conjoined element following the negated element is to emphasize the absence of availing.

The meaning of "from Allah" (min Allah) is "from the might of Allah or from His punishment." The omission of the like of this is common in speech, and its estimation is evident. Scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) call this usage "attributing a ruling to objects while intending their most well-known states," such as ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], i.e., its eating.

The clause ﴿Their wealth will not avail them﴾ etc. is a third or second predicate of "inna" in His saying, ﴿Indeed, they are evil in what they used to do﴾ [al-Mujadila: 15].

The clause ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾ occupies the position of a cause for the clause ﴿Their wealth and their children will not avail them against Allah at all﴾, i.e., because they are the companions of the Fire, meaning it is established for them that they are the companions of the Fire. The companion of a thing is one who is constantly with it and does not part from it. Since it has been established in His saying, ﴿Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment﴾ [al-Mujadila: 15], and in His saying, ﴿For them is a humiliating punishment﴾ [al-Mujadila: 16], that there is no escape for them from the Fire, how then could their wealth and children avail them anything against the punishment of the Fire? This is like His saying, ﴿Then is one upon whom the word of punishment has come [equal to one who will be saved]? Would you then save one who is in the Fire?﴾ [al-Zumar: 19], i.e., you cannot save him from the Fire. Indeed, the demonstrative in such a position alerts that the one indicated has become deserving of what follows the demonstrative, because of the reports that were given about him before the demonstrative, as has preceded in His saying, ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 58, verse 18:

﴿On the Day when Allah resurrects them all, and they swear to Him as they swear to you, and they think that they are upon something. Verily, it is they who are the liars.﴾

This is connected to His saying ﴿and they swear to a lie﴾ [al-Mujadila: 14] up to His saying ﴿they have taken their oaths as a shield﴾ [al-Mujadila: 16]. The discussion of the like of His saying ﴿on the Day when Allah resurrects them all, then He will inform them of what they did﴾ has already passed, as mentioned earlier in this surah; that is, remember the Day when Allah resurrects them.

Their swearing to Allah in the Hereafter is an allusion to what Allah related about them in His saying ﴿Then their trial was only that they said, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾ [al-An'am: 23].

The comparison in His saying ﴿as they swear to you﴾ is in respect of the manner of the oath, which is their saying that they are not polytheists, and in its being an oath upon a lie while they know it. For this reason, the Exalted called it a trial (fitnah) in the verse of al-An'am: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Then their trial was only that they said, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾ [al-An'am: 23].

The meaning of ﴿and they think that they are upon something﴾ is that they will suppose on that day that their oath will benefit them with acceptance before Allah, so they think they have obtained something great, that is, something beneficial.

"Upon" (ʿalā) here is for the figurative sense of elevation, which is the intensity of being characterized by an attribute and the like, as in His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] in the Surah al-Baqarah.

The word "thing" (shay') has its qualifying adjective omitted because its meaning is clear from the context; that is, upon something beneficial, like His, Exalted is He, ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, you are not upon anything until you establish the Torah and the Gospel."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 68]. And like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ when he was asked about the soothsayers: "They are nothing" (laysu bi-shay'in).

This implies their deep immersion in hypocrisy, their persistence in it, and that it remains in their souls after their resurrection, because their selves emerged from the world of this life characterized by it. Souls acquire purification or corruption only in the world of obligation. The wisdom of creating souls in this world is their purification and the clarifying of their turbidity, so that they may reach the world of eternity pure. If they travel the path of purification, they arrive at the world of eternity purified, and Allah increases them in purity and training on the Day of Resurrection. If they are immersed during life in the mire of deficiencies and the clay of vices, they come on the Day of Resurrection in the state they were in, their condition disfigured, so that they become a mockery for the people of the gathering. Some qualities that do not contradict virtue and do not oppose the world of reality may remain in purified souls, such as lawful desires and meeting loved ones. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿The intimate friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67]. ﴿O My servants, no fear shall be upon you today, nor shall you grieve﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 68]. ﴿Those who believed in Our signs and were Muslims﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 69]. ﴿Enter Paradise, you and your spouses, delighted﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 70].

In a hadith, the Prophet ﷺ said: "A man from the people of Paradise asks his Lord for permission to cultivate. Allah says: 'Are you not in what you wish?' He says: 'Yes, but I love to cultivate.' So he hastens, sows, and its growth, its maturity, its harvesting and its piling up become like mountains, as the blink of an eye." A man from the desert dwellers was with the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we do not find this except Qurashi or Ansari, for they are the people of farming; as for us, we are not people of farming." The Prophet ﷺ laughed, affirming what the Bedouin had understood.

In the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah in Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Every servant is resurrected upon what he died upon." 'Iyad said in al-Ikmal: it is general in every state in which a person dies. al-Suyuti said: "The flute player will be resurrected with his flute, and the wine drinker with his cup." End quote. I say: then the realities will be unveiled to them as they truly are, for knowledge will become according to reality.

He concluded this discourse with His saying ﴿Verily, it is they who are the liars﴾, which is a comprehensive conclusion regarding their lying which Allah mentioned in His saying ﴿and they swear to a lie﴾ [al-Mujadila: 14]. The meaning is that their lie against you is not matched by any lie, so the description of being liars is restricted to them by the pronoun of separation in His saying ﴿Verily, it is they who are the liars﴾. This is a claimed restriction for emphasis, since the lying of others is not counted. He reinforced this with the particle of emphasis, to affirm the meaning of the claimed restriction, namely that the lying of others is as nothing beside their lying; and with the opening particle, which calls the hearing to their report, to establish how firmly the attribute of lying is rooted in them, to the extent that it clings to them on the Day of Resurrection.

[Page 54]

This is a resumptive explanatory clause (*isti'naf bayani*, a clause that answers a question the preceding words naturally raise). The description of them, restricting the quality of lying to them, prompts the listener to ask about the cause that brought them to this dreadful state. The answer is that it is the domination of Satan over them and his possession of the reins of their souls, so that he directs them however he wishes. Would Satan be content with anything less than the worst corruption and misguidance?

*Istihwadh* means seizure and overpowering. It is the form *istif'al* from *hadha*, *yahudhu hawdhan*, meaning to surround a thing and direct it as one wishes. One says *hadha al-'ira* when he gathers and drives the caravan, overpowering it. From this they derived the form *istaf'ala* for one who takes control through management and effort. For this reason *istihwadh* is said only of the taking control by a rational being, since it requires means of control. Its synonym is *istawla*. The *sin* and *ta'* serve to intensify the sense of overpowering, as they do in *istajaba*.

*Al-ahwadhi* means one who masters difficult matters. 'A'isha said: "'Umar was *ahwadhi*, unmatched in his kind."

The original form of *istahwadha* should have been that its middle radical be changed to an *alif*, because its root is a *waw* that is vowelled after a sound quiescent letter. This is not a form of exclamation, nor a doubled-final-radical verb, nor a weak-final-radical verb. Therefore its vowel should be moved to the sound quiescent letter before it, to avoid the heaviness of a vowel on a weak letter, while keeping that vowel by transferring it to the letter before it, which is free of vowel. The weak letter then remains quiescent with a dead sukun after a vowel, and is changed into a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding vowel, as in *yaqumu*, *yabinu* and *aqama*. So the regular form would be *istaha<u>dh</u>a*, but the eloquent usage is to keep it sound against the usual pattern of its class. This is a transmitted (*sama'i*) retention, and it has few parallels, such as *istanwaqa al-jamalu* (the camel became like a female camel), *a'wala* (he raised his voice), *aghyamat al-sama'* (the sky became cloudy), and *istaghyala al-sabiyyu* (the child drank *ghayl*, which is the milk of a nursing mother). Abu Zayd said that retention is a dialect of some Arabs, consistently applied throughout this entire class. The exegetes report that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab recited *istaha<u>dh</u>a 'alayhimu al-shaytanu* (with the *alif*). Al-Jawhari said: the retention of this entire class is consistent. In *al-Tashil*, it is said: the retention of this class is consistently applied to every verb whose triliteral form is unused, such as *istanwaqa al-jamalu* and *istatyasat al-shatu*, when she became like a male goat.

The discussion of *al-istihwadh* has already been given under the words of His Exalted Saying: ﴿They said: Did we not have mastery over you and protect you from the believers?﴾ (Surah al-Nisa, 4:141). So this is joined to that.

The forgetting intended here is its implication, which is neglect and abandonment of what is forgotten, in accordance with His Exalted Saying: ﴿Thus came Our signs to you, but you forgot them, and thus today you are forgotten﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha, 20:126).

*Al-dhikr* is used for the utterance of the tongue, with a name or speech, and it is also used for remembrance by the intellect. The second meaning is sometimes specified by the *dhal* with a damma (*al-dhikr*). Here it is used in both its literal and figurative sense, that is, it is used in its implication, which is worship and obedience. The meaning is that He made them forget the Oneness of God, through the word of testimony, and turning towards Him in worship. One who does not remember anything does not turn to his duties.

The clause ﴿Those are the party of Satan﴾ is a consequence and summary of the phrase ﴿Satan has taken possession of them﴾, since taking possession requires that he has made them among his followers. The demonstrative pronoun serves to add distinction to them, lest there be doubt that they are the party of Satan.

The clause ﴿Surely the party of Satan are the losers﴾ comes in the position of a branching and causal consequence of the clause ﴿Those are the party of Satan﴾. The apparent form would have been "For the party of Satan are the losers," but He turned away from that to the opening particle (*alla*), to draw attention to the importance of its content and that it deserves to be firmly fixed in minds, in emphatic warning against joining them and taking on the states of conduct mentioned just before. This warning is intensified by emphasizing the statement with the particle *inna* and by the restrictive form, since no one doubts that the party of Satan are losers. This is among the established truths among people. Therefore these emphases were not for refuting denial, but to warn the believers that the snares of Satan should not deceive them, that the outward show of the hypocrites should not appeal to their eyes, and that their false oaths should not mislead them.

The explicit mention of the phrase ﴿the party of Satan﴾ instead of a pronoun is for greater clarity, and so that the sentence is suitable to be used as a standalone proverb, independent in its meaning.

The pronoun of separation (*damir al-fasl*, the pronoun "hum" between subject and predicate) conveys restriction (*qasr*). It is a claimed restriction (*qasr idda'i*), for emphasis on the extent of their loss, and that there is no loss more severe than it. So every other loss is considered as nothing, and it is claimed that the quality of being a loser is restricted to them.

The *hizb* of a person is his helpers, his army, and those who support him.

﴿Surely those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, they are among the most humiliated.﴾ ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail. Surely Allah is Strong, Mighty."﴾.

The placement of this verse after what was mentioned of the hypocrites' conditions resembles the placement of the verse ﴿Surely those who oppose Allah and His Messenger will be humiliated, as those before them were humiliated﴾ [al-Mujadila: 5]. So "those who oppose Allah and His Messenger" previously mentioned refers to the polytheists who openly opposed them (muhadda, hostility). As for the opponents mentioned in this verse, they are those who conceal their opposition while outwardly showing allegiance, namely the hypocrites (al-munafiqun). The sentence is therefore an explanatory resumptive sentence (istinaf bayani, a sentence that answers an implied question), which clarifies part of the loss that Allah has decreed upon the party of Satan (hizb al-shaytan), of whom they are the vanguard. By this, the sentence takes on the sense of a partial substitution (badal al-ba'd, a substitute that is only part of the preceding content) of the content of the sentence ﴿Surely the party of Satan are the losers﴾ [al-Mujadila: 19], because loss occurs in this world and the Hereafter, and the loss of this world has types, the most severe of which for people is humiliation and defeat. The meaning is: the party of Satan are among the humiliated and vanquished.

Their being brought to mind through the relative clause ﴿those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Mujadila: 5] is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun (izhar fi maqam al-idmar). The apparent expectation was to say: "They are among the humiliated," but the speech departed from what the apparent context requires to the relative form (mawsuliyya), to convey the implication of the relative clause, that they are enemies of Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ). The relative form also indicates the reason for the judgment that follows it, namely that they are humiliated, because they are enemies of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Thus they are enemies of Allah, who is capable of everything, and His enemy cannot be mighty.

The particle of location (harf al-zarfiyya, "in") indicates that they are included within the group described as humiliated, that is, those who are extremely humiliated, so that the listener imagines them in every group he sees as humiliated. Therefore this structure is more eloquent than saying: "Those are the humiliated."

The demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah, "those") is an alert that those being referred to deserve what follows the demonstrative in terms of judgment, because of the attribute that precedes it, like ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 5].

The discussion of ﴿those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Mujadila: 5] has already passed at the beginning of this surah.

The sentence ﴿Allah has decreed: "I will surely prevail"﴾ is a cause (illah) for the sentence ﴿those are among the humiliated﴾, meaning: because Allah

wanted His Messenger (ﷺ) to prevail over his enemies, and that is one of the effects of the power of Allah, which nothing can overcome. He has decreed victory for all His messengers over their enemies, so their victory is from the victory of Allah, since the power of Allah is related to things in accordance with the will of Allah, which nothing changes. The will follows knowledge, and the totality of the coming together of knowledge, will and power over what exists is what is called the decree (qada'). It is what is expressed here by "Allah has decreed" (kataba Allah), because writing (kitaba) is used metaphorically (istu'īra) for the meaning: Allah has decided that and willed its occurrence at the time He knows and wills it. So it is certain to occur and does not fail, like a matter that one wants to record and keep unchanged; it is written so that it is not forgotten, nothing is reduced from it, and the agreement upon it is not denied.

Thus victory is established for His Messenger (ﷺ), since what Allah decreed for His messengers includes him. This is a demonstrative proof (burhani) of the victory of His Messenger over peoples who oppose him.

The phrase ﴿I will surely prevail﴾ is formulated in the form of speech (sigha al-qawl), as a complement (tarshih, a supporting detail completing the metaphor) to the metaphor of "wrote" in the sense of "decreed and determined." The meaning is: He decreed the content of this sentence, that is, He decreed victory for Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ). It is as if this sentence is what was written by Allah. The apparent expectation was to say: "They are among the humiliated," but the speech departed from what the apparent context requires to the relative form (mawsuliyya), to convey the implication of the relative clause, that they are enemies of Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ). The relative form also indicates the reason for the judgment that follows it, namely that they are humiliated, because they are enemies of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Thus they are enemies of Allah, who is capable of everything, and His enemy cannot be mighty.

The particle of location (harf al-zarfiyya, "in") indicates that they are included within the group described as humiliated, that is, those who are extremely humiliated, so that the listener imagines them in every group he sees as humiliated. Therefore this structure is more eloquent than saying: "Those are the humiliated."

The demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah, "those") is an alert that those being referred to deserve what follows the demonstrative in terms of judgment, because of the attribute that precedes it, like ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 5].

The discussion of ﴿those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Mujadila: 5] has already passed at the beginning of this surah.

The sentence ﴿Allah has decreed: "I will surely prevail"﴾ is a cause (illah) for the sentence ﴿those are among the humiliated﴾, meaning: because Allah

[Page 57]

wanted His Messenger (ﷺ) to prevail over his enemies, and that is one of the effects of the power of Allah, which nothing can overcome. He has decreed victory for all His messengers over their enemies, so their victory is from the victory of Allah, since the power of Allah is related to things in accordance with the will of Allah, which nothing changes. The will follows knowledge, and the totality of the coming together of knowledge, will and power over what exists is what is called the decree (qada'). It is what is expressed here by "Allah has decreed" (kataba Allah), because writing (kitaba) is used metaphorically (istu'īra) for the meaning: Allah has decided that and willed its occurrence at the time He knows and wills it. So it is certain to occur and does not fail, like a matter that one wants to record and keep unchanged; it is written so that it is not forgotten, nothing is reduced from it, and the agreement upon it is not denied.

Thus victory is established for His Messenger (ﷺ), since what Allah decreed for His messengers includes him. This is a demonstrative proof (burhani) of the victory of His Messenger over peoples who oppose him.

The phrase ﴿I will surely prevail﴾ is formulated in the form of speech (sigha al-qawl), as a complement (tarshih, a supporting detail completing the metaphor) to the metaphor of "wrote" in the sense of "decreed and determined." The meaning is: He decreed the content of this sentence, that is, He decreed victory for Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ). It is as if this sentence is what was written by Allah. What is meant is victory by force, because the speech is directed as a threat. As for victory by argument, it is a known matter.

The sentence ﴿Surely Allah is Strong, Mighty﴾ is a reason (ta'lil) for the sentence ﴿I will surely prevail﴾, because whoever overcomes the victor is himself vanquished. Hassan said:

"Sukhayna claimed that it would overcome its Lord,
but the overcomer of the Overpowerer shall surely be overcome."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 58, verse 22 (part 1 of 2):

﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their kinsfolk.﴾

There were among the hypocrites (munafiqin) kinship ties with many of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, and their hypocrisy was not hidden from some of them. So Allah warned the sincere believers against showing affection to those who are hostile to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.

Eight reports of varying chain strength were transmitted concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, which al-Qurtubi surveyed.

It is not necessary that the verse have an occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), for its apparent meaning is that it is connected in meaning with what precedes and follows it, namely the censure of the hypocrites and their allegiance to the Jews. Whatever stories are mentioned concerning its occasion of revelation are merely examples of what its ruling requires.

The opening of the speech with ﴿You will not find a people﴾ arouses eagerness to know the condition of these people and the ruling that will be laid down concerning them.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and its purpose is to command him to convey to the Muslims that showing affection to one who is known to be an opponent of Allah and His Messenger is something that contradicts faith, so that whoever might be engaged in it would refrain from it. The speech is thus, by way of metonymy (kinaya), a means of negating the finding of a people with this description, like the saying: "Let me not see you here," meaning: "Do not be present here."

From this is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say: Will you inform Allah of what He does not know in the heavens or on the earth?﴾ [Yunus: 18]. He meant by "what He does not know" what does not exist, because what Allah does not know cannot possibly exist. This was the habit of the believers before the Hijra, during the days when they were in Mecca. Reports from evidences of this have been transmitted, of varying strength, but unbelief was at that time manifest and enmity between the believers and the polytheists was clear. When the Muslims moved to Medina, unbelief was concealed within the hypocrites, so guarding against their affection was more fitting and more cautious.

Al-mawadda (affection) originally means the existence of affection on both sides. The prohibition here is only against the affection of a believer for unbelievers, not against the unbeliever's returning affection to the believers. The form of mufa'ala (tawadda) is used here in consideration that the nature of affection is to bring forth affection from the beloved toward the lover.

Alternatively, the mufa'ala may be a metonymy for the affection being sincere, because the sincere lover is met with the like of his affection from the beloved. This is known from evidences of the dealings, and the indication of the metonymy is the directing of the negation of finding one described by this to the people who believe in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. For this reason Allah did not say here ﴿except that you fear from them a fear (taqiyya)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28], because affection is one of the states of the heart, so taqiyya cannot be conceived along with it, unlike His saying ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28], up to His saying ﴿except that you fear from them a fear﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28].

His saying ﴿even if they were their fathers﴾ to the end is an exaggeration regarding the furthest of the circumstances in which a person might be inclined to permit what has been forbidden on account of the closeness of kinship.

Moreover, one who opposes Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, if he is openly and manifestly so, or openly displays ill treatment of the Muslims because of their Islam and not because of a worldly enmity, then it is obligatory upon the Muslims to show their enmity toward him. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah only forbids you from those who fight you over religion, drive you out of your homes, and support others in driving you out, that you make allies of them; and whoever makes allies of them, then it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾ [Al-Mumtahana: 9]. Dealing with them kindly was permitted only to protect oneself from their evil, if they had power, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers; and whoever does that has nothing with Allah, except that you fear from them a fear﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28].

As for others than this category, they are the disbelievers who restrain their evil from the Muslims. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not drive you out of your homes, from being righteous toward them and acting justly toward them. Indeed, Allah loves the just﴾ [Al-Mumtahana: 8].

Among this category are the people of dhimma (ahl al-dhimma). Shihab al-Din al-Qarafi, in the nineteenth and hundredth difference (al-Farq al-tasi' 'ashar ba'da al-mi'a), explained the matters distinguishing righteousness (al-birr) from affection (al-mawadda). With this you know that this verse is not abrogated by the verse ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion﴾ [Al-Mumtahana: 8], and that each of them has its own situation.

Fa (in "fa-law") is for connection, and the meaning of the connective "law" (law al-wasliyya) was already explained at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold even if he offered it as ransom﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91] in Surat Al 'Imran. The categories of kinship in this verse are arranged in a descending manner from the strongest to what is less than it, lest it be supposed that the prohibition is specific to the one in whom there is a suspicion of giving him counsel and obeying his command.

The clan (ashira) of a man is his tribe, those with whom he gathers in a not-distant ancestor. The scholars have derived from this verse that people of complete faith do not show affection to anyone in whom there is a meaning of opposing Allah and His Messenger ﷺ by breaching the fence of His Sharia deliberately and treating the sanctities of Islam lightly. Such people are like the people of injustice and aggression in deeds, of every kind that indicates little regard for religion by its doer and reveals weak reverence for religion, like those who openly display major sins and abominations, mocking the admonitions and sermons,

and like the people of deviation and error in belief, whose condition indicates turning away from the proofs of the true belief, and preferring personal desire and partisanship over the proofs of the true Islamic belief. From al-Thawri it is related that he said: "They used to regard this verse as applying to those who keep company with rulers of oppression." From Malik: "Do not sit with the Qadariyya, and be hostile to them for the sake of Allah, because of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾."

Our jurists said: It is permissible or obligatory to shun the possessor of a misguided innovation (bid'a), or one who immerses himself in major sins, if he does not accept admonition.

All of this is from giving some of the rulings of a meaning in which there is a legal ruling or a threat to another meaning in which there is a description of the same kind as the meaning bearing the established ruling. This goes back to kinds of resemblance (shabah) in the paths of effective cause (masalik al-'illa) for analogy, for things vary in their resemblance.

The leading scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (a'imma al-usul) have also used His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows other than the way of the believers—We will give him what he has taken and expose him to Hell﴾ [An-Nisa: 115], as evidence for the authority of consensus (hujjiyyat al-ijma'), although the apparent subject of the verse they cite is in fact departure from Islam. But they considered departure to have varying degrees, so opposing the consensus of all the Muslims contains a resemblance to following other than the way of the believers.

﴿Those—He has written within their hearts faith and supported them with a spirit from Him, and He will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. Those are the party of Allah. Unquestionably, the party of Allah are the successful.﴾

The demonstrative refers to the people described as ﴿believing in Allah and the Last Day, loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their kinsfolk﴾.

The sentence is resumed as an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because the preceding descriptions, and their occurrence after what was described of the hypocrites regarding opposing Allah and His Messenger ﷺ previously and just now, and what Allah threatened them with—that He has prepared for them a severe punishment and for them a humiliating punishment, and that they are the party of Satan, and that they are the losers—prompts the hearer to look forward to what will be told about those characterized by the opposite of that. They are the believers who do not show affection to those who oppose Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.

The writing of faith in the hearts is like His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: I will surely prevail, I and My messengers﴾ [Al-Mujadila: 21]. It is the firm decree whose effects are not averted; that is, they are the believers in truth, whom Allah has adorned with faith in their hearts, so they follow its perfection and tread its path.

Ta'yid (support): strengthening and aid. Its explanation was already given at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We supported him with the Holy Spirit﴾ [Al-Baqara: 87] in Surat al-Baqara. That is, Allah's support of them has already occurred and been established by the use of the past tense, to indicate occurrence, certainty and permanence, so it is used in both its meanings.

The spirit here is that by which the perfection of a thing's kind is achieved, whether action or otherwise; and "a spirit from Him" is His care and gentleness. The meanings of "spirit" appear at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And they ask you about the spirit﴾ [Al-Isra: 85] in Surat al-Isra. And He promised them that He will admit them in the future to gardens, abiding therein.

His being pleased with them is something attained from the past and of established permanence, so it is like the past in His saying "and supported them." Their being pleased with their Lord is likewise attained in this world through their steadfastness upon the religion and their enmity toward its enemies, and it is attained in the future through the attainment of Allah's pleasure with them and the attainment of the bliss of eternity.

As for changing the expression to the present tense in His saying ﴿and He will admit them to gardens﴾, it is because the present tense is the basic form for the future. The meaning of confirmation has been dispensed with by what precedes it, His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Those—He has written within their hearts faith and supported them with a spirit from Him﴾.

His saying ﴿Those are the party of Allah﴾ to the end is like the statement regarding ﴿Those are the party of Satan﴾ [Al-Mujadila: 19]. The particle of alerting (harf al-tanbih) produces an alert of the Muslims to their merit, and an alert of whoever hears that among the hypocrites to what Allah has bestowed upon the Muslims of the good of this world and the Hereafter, perhaps the hypocrites would envy them and thereby sincerely embrace Islam.

How far apart are the two parties! Loss belongs to the party of Satan, and success belongs to the party of Allah, Exalted is He.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Surat al-Hashr. This surah is famously named (Surat al-Hashr), and by this name the Prophet ﷺ called it.

al-Tirmidhi related from Ma'qil ibn Yasar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever says three times in the morning, 'I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan,' and recites three verses from the end of Surat al-Hashr..." the hadith, meaning the verses whose first is ﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ [Al-Hashr: 22] to the end of the surah.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas, "Surat al-Hashr," and he said, "Say: Surat Bani al-Nadir." So Ibn Jubayr named it by its well-known name, while Ibn 'Abbas called it Surat Bani al-Nadir. Perhaps the naming by the Prophet ﷺ of it as (Surat al-Hashr) had not reached him, because the apparent sense of his speech is that he regarded its name as Surat Bani al-Nadir, given his saying to Ibn Jubayr, "Say: Bani al-Nadir."

Ibn Hajar interpreted Ibn 'Abbas's words as meaning that he disliked naming it (al-Hashr), lest one suppose that by al-Hashr is meant the Day of Resurrection. This is a distant interpretation. Better than this is that Ibn 'Abbas meant that it has two names, and that the imperative in his saying "Say" is for choice (al-takhyir).

As for the reason it is named (al-Hashr), it is because the word (al-hashr) occurs in it, and because in it is mentioned

the mustering (hashr) of Bani al-Nadir from their dwellings, that is, from their town called al-Zuhra near Medina. They went out to the lands of Syria, to Ariha and Adhri'at, and some of their households went out to Khaybar, and some of their households went out to al-Hira.

As for the reason it is named Surat Bani al-Nadir, it is because the story of Bani al-Nadir is mentioned in it.

It is Medinan by consensus.

It is the ninety-eighth in the reckoning of the order of the revelation of the surahs according to Jabir ibn Zayd. It was revealed after Surat al-Bayyina and before Surat al-Nasr.

Its revelation took place immediately after the expulsion of Bani al-Nadir from their lands, in the fourth year after the Hijra.

The number of its verses is twenty-four, by agreement of the counters.

There is consensus that it was revealed concerning the affair of Bani al-Nadir, but they did not specify what the purpose was for which it was revealed. It appears that its aim is the ruling on the property of Bani al-Nadir after victory over them, as we will explain in the commentary on its first verse.

It has included that what is in the heavens and what is on the earth points to God's transcendence (tanzih), to the fact that the heavens and the earth belong to His dominion (mulk), and that He is the Almighty (al-Ghalib) and the Governor (al-Mudabbir).

And it recalls God's favor in facilitating the expulsion (ijla') of the Banu al-Nadir despite their strength (al-mana'ah), their fortresses (husun), and their equipment (al-'uddah). That is one of the signs of the support (ta'yid) of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and of his victory over his enemies.

It also recalls what the Muslims carried out in destroying the property of the Banu al-Nadir, the rulings on that property, and the specification of its rightful recipients among the Muslims.

It exalts the status of the Muhajirun, the Ansar, and those who come after them among the believers.

It uncovers the hidden intentions (dakha'il) of the hypocrites (munafiqun) and their promises to the Banu al-Nadir that they would support them, and how they broke their promise to them.

It condemns the Banu al-Nadir and the hypocrites for cowardice (jubn) and disunity (tafarruq al-kalimah), and draws a parallel between the deception of the hypocrites toward the Jews and the deception of Satan toward those who disbelieve in God, and Satan's disavowal of that on the Day of Resurrection. So the final outcome for all of them is eternal abiding in the Fire.

Then comes the address to the believers, commanding them to be mindful of God (taqwa) and to beware of the states of the companions of the Fire, and reminding them of the difference between the two groups.

It also explains the greatness and majesty of the Qur'an and that it requires the humility (khushu') of its people.

Interwoven within this is an allusion to the wisdom behind the laws of transferring property among Muslims through the means that Islam has organized, in such a way that they do not burden the owners of property.

And it commands following what God legislates through the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ).

It concludes with great divine attributes, and [mentions] that whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him, as a purification of the state of the believers and an indirect reproach to the disbelievers.
